unique case with default
Yosys and Verilator read the comment, Icarus Verilog ignores it


.v, read_verilog, iverilog
.sv, read_verilog -sv, iverilog -g2012
Verilator reads both as SystemVerilog






Most of these differences are syntax, but three of them matter beyond syntax:

reg and wire follow the assignment, not the hardware. In Verilog, a signal assigned in an always block must be a reg, even if it is combinational, and a signal driven by an assign or by an instance must be a wire. If you turn an assign into an always block, you therefore have to change the declaration as well. In SystemVerilog, a variable (logic or reg) may be assigned in an always block or by a single assign, so the declaration stays the same, and no type name suggests a register that does not exist. Only a wire assigned in an always block remains an error (Icarus Verilog: not a valid l-value, Verilator: PROCASSWIRE for an internal wire).
The process types state the intent. For a missing assignment in always @(*), Verilator and Yosys 0.70 only warn, and Yosys builds the latch. For always_comb, Yosys stops with an error (Section 2.5.8).
Checks belong in the language, not in comments. In Verilog, the comment // synopsys full_case parallel_case after a case tells the synthesis tool that all missing values are don’t care (full_case) and that the items never overlap (parallel_case). Yosys reads it and builds no latch, and Verilator reads it as well: it drops the LATCH and CASEINCOMPLETE warnings and stops the simulation when no item matches. Icarus Verilog ignores the comment and keeps the old value, so its simulation can differ from the netlist. Write a complete case with a default item instead, and add unique if the items are mutually exclusive. Keep the default with unique as well. Without it, Yosys handles unique like full_case: it silently takes the missing values as don’t care, even in always_comb, and the netlist can differ from the simulation.

Most testbench features of this chapter are SystemVerilog as well, e.g., $fatal, $isunknown(), and int variables, and the verification part of the language (classes, randomization, assertions, and coverage) has no Verilog counterpart.
Finally, the tools must know which language they read. Verilator reads every file as SystemVerilog, also a .v file. Icarus Verilog reads Verilog-2005 unless you select SystemVerilog with -g2012, and the Yosys command read_verilog needs the option -sv, even for a file that ends in .sv. Name your files .sv, so that readers and editors know which language is inside.






TipExercise: Modernize a Verilog-2001 Module



The following priority encoder with registered outputs is written in plain Verilog-2001, as you find it in many older designs: idx is the index of the lowest set bit of req, and valid is high if any bit of req is set. Besides its old style, the module contains one mistake.


prio_enc/verilog/prio_enc.v

// SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Simon Dorrer
// SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
// Description: Priority encoder with registered outputs in plain
// Verilog-2001. idx is the index of the lowest set bit of req,
// valid is high if any bit of req is set. This file contains a
// mistake on purpose (exercise), do not use it as a template.

module prio_enc (clk, rst_n, req, idx, valid);

  parameter N = 8;
  parameter W = 3;  // width of idx, must be log2(N)

  input          clk;
  input          rst_n;
  input  [N-1:0] req;
  output [W-1:0] idx;
  output         valid;

  reg    [W-1:0] idx;
  reg            valid;
  reg    [W-1:0] idx_next;
  wire           valid_next;
  integer        i;

  always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
    if (!rst_n) begin
      idx   <= {W{1'b0}};
      valid <= 1'b0;
    end else begin
      idx   <= idx_next;
      valid <= valid_next;
    end
  end

  assign valid_next = |req;

  // The loop runs from the highest to the lowest bit, so the
  // lowest set bit is assigned last and wins.
  always @(*) begin
    for (i = N - 1; i >= 0; i = i - 1)
      if (req[i])
        idx_next = i;
  end

endmodule



Which constructs are plain Verilog, and what are their SystemVerilog counterparts in Table 15?
Save the file as prio_enc.v, lint it with verilator --lint-only -Wall prio_enc.v, and synthesize it with yosys -p "read_verilog prio_enc.v; synth -top prio_enc; stat". What do the two tools report?
Translate the module into SystemVerilog in prio_enc.sv, with the conventions of this chapter: ANSI ports with _i and _o, rst_ni, logic, and the two-process style with _d and _q. Do not fix the mistake yet. Synthesize your translation with read_verilog -sv. What has changed?
Fix the mistake and the remaining lint warning, and lint and synthesize the module again.



Before continuing, please finish the previous exercise. Once you are done, compare with the solution below.






TipSolution: Modernize a Verilog-2001 Module






Each plain Verilog construct and its SystemVerilog counterpart:

The port list with separate declarations (Verilog-1995 style) becomes an ANSI header with logic ports.
The regs (the outputs and idx_next, assigned in always blocks) and the wire valid_next (driven by an assign) all become logic.
always @(*) and always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) become always_comb and always_ff.
The module-level integer i with i = i - 1 becomes for (int i = N - 1; i >= 0; i--).
The replication {W{1'b0}} becomes '0.
The untyped parameters become parameter int unsigned, and W, which must be set to match N by hand, becomes $clog2(N).
The file extension .v becomes .sv.

Verilator 5.052 reports two warnings. WIDTHTRUNC: the 32-bit integer i is assigned to the 3-bit idx_next. LATCH: if no bit of req is set, the loop assigns nothing, and idx_next keeps its old value. Yosys 0.70 only prints the warning Latch inferred for signal `\prio_enc.\idx_next' and builds 23 cells, among them four flip-flops $_DFF_PN0_ for idx and valid and three latches $_DLATCH_N_ for idx_next. Leaving a value unassigned does not mean “don’t care” but “keep the old value.”
With always_comb, Yosys stops with ERROR: Latch inferred for signal `\prio_enc.\idx_d' from always_comb process. Verilator reports the same LATCH warning as before, and WIDTHTRUNC again unless your translation already casts i.
The fix is a default assignment, as in every combinational process of this chapter:



prio_enc/rtl/prio_enc.sv

// SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Simon Dorrer
// SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
// Description: Priority encoder with registered outputs. idx_o
// is the index of the lowest set bit of req_i, valid_o is high if
// any bit of req_i is set.

`default_nettype none

module prio_enc #(
  parameter int unsigned N = 8
) (
  input  logic                 clk_i,
  input  logic                 rst_ni,
  input  logic [N-1:0]         req_i,
  output logic [$clog2(N)-1:0] idx_o,
  output logic                 valid_o
);

  localparam int unsigned W = $clog2(N);

  logic [W-1:0] idx_d, idx_q;
  logic         valid_d, valid_q;

  // Register process: reset values and copies of the _d signals only
  always_ff @(posedge clk_i or negedge rst_ni) begin
    if (!rst_ni) begin
      idx_q   <= '0;
      valid_q <= 1'b0;
    end else begin
      idx_q   <= idx_d;
      valid_q <= valid_d;
    end
  end

  // Combinational process: defaults first, then all decisions
  always_comb begin
    idx_d   = '0;
    valid_d = |req_i;
    // The loop runs from the highest to the lowest bit, so the
    // lowest set bit is assigned last and wins.
    for (int i = N - 1; i >= 0; i--) begin
      if (req_i[i]) begin
        idx_d = W'(i);
      end
    end
  end

  assign idx_o   = idx_q;
  assign valid_o = valid_q;

endmodule

`default_nettype wire



The width W follows from N with $clog2 (available since Verilog-2005), so it can no longer be set wrong.
The size cast W'(i) makes the truncation of the loop variable explicit.
The loop variable is declared in the loop. It must be a signed int: with int unsigned, the condition i >= 0 is always true. Verilator 5.052 reports a constant comparison (UNSIGNED) and an infinite loop (INFINITELOOP) and then stops with an internal error.

Verilator reports no warning, and Yosys builds 22 cells with the four flip-flops and no latch. While valid_o is low, idx_o is now 0, where the original kept the last index (or x before the first request). This does not matter, since idx_o is only meaningful while valid_o is high. The default idx_d = idx_q; would also be correct: it keeps the last index in the register, and Yosys turns the three idx flip-flops into flip-flops with enable ($_DFFE_PN0P_), again without a latch.
The testbench prio_enc/testbenches/verilog/prio_enc_tb.sv in the code folder applies all 256 values of req and compares the outputs with a reference model, checking idx_o only while valid_o is high. It also runs with your own translation, as long as it has the parameter N and the ports clk_i, rst_ni, req_i, idx_o, and valid_o. Copy it next to your translation, and run it:
T=/foss/designs/vlsi-design/content/sv_crashcourse/code/prio_enc
cp $T/testbenches/verilog/prio_enc_tb.sv .
iverilog -g2012 -o prio_enc_tb.vvp prio_enc.sv prio_enc_tb.sv
vvp prio_enc_tb.vvp

title: VLSI Design
text:
2.6 Testbenches
A testbench applies stimuli to the design under test (DUT) and checks its responses. It is simulation-only code, so it may use the whole language. Make every testbench self-checking: it compares the outputs with the expected values and reports a clear pass or fail, so that you never have to judge a waveform by eye to know whether a design works. Waveforms are for debugging. This section shows a SystemVerilog and a cocotb testbench for the tick generator of Section 2.5.7. Section 4 covers verification with cocotb in depth.

2.6.1 A SystemVerilog Testbench


tick_gen/testbenches/verilog/tick_gen_tb.sv

// SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Simon Dorrer
// SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
// Description: Self-checking SystemVerilog testbench for tick_gen.

`timescale 1ns / 1ps

module tick_gen_tb;

  localparam int unsigned DIV           = 5;
  localparam real         CLK_PERIOD_NS = 20.0;  // 50 MHz

  logic clk   = 1'b0;
  logic rst_n = 1'b0;  // reset is active from time 0
  logic en    = 1'b0;
  logic tick;

  // Device under test (DUT)
  tick_gen #(
    .DIV(DIV)
  ) dut (
    .clk_i (clk),
    .rst_ni(rst_n),
    .en_i  (en),
    .tick_o(tick)
  );

  // Clock generation
  always #(CLK_PERIOD_NS / 2) clk = ~clk;

  // Stimulus and checks: inputs change and outputs are sampled on the
  // falling edge, so they never race with the DUT at the rising edge.
  initial begin
    $dumpfile("tick_gen_tb.vcd");
    $dumpvars(0, tick_gen_tb);

    repeat (2) @(negedge clk);
    rst_n = 1'b1;

    // Disabled: no tick at all
    repeat (3 * DIV) begin
      @(negedge clk);
      if (tick !== 1'b0) $fatal(1, "FAIL: tick while disabled");
    end

    // Enabled: exactly one tick every DIV clock cycles
    en = 1'b1;
    for (int cycle = 1; cycle <= 4 * DIV; cycle++) begin
      @(negedge clk);
      if (tick !== (cycle % DIV == 0)) begin
        $fatal(1, "FAIL: cycle %0d, tick = %b", cycle, tick);
      end
    end

    $display("PASS: tick_gen_tb");
    $finish;
  end

endmodule



`timescale 1ns / 1ps sets the unit of the delays (#) and the precision of the simulation.
The testbench is a module without ports. It instantiates the DUT with a smaller DIV than the default, which keeps the simulation short.
always #(CLK_PERIOD_NS / 2) clk = ~clk; generates the clock. Initial values in declarations are fine in a testbench.
The stimulus runs in an initial block. Inputs are changed and outputs are checked on the falling clock edge (@(negedge clk)), while the DUT acts on the rising edge. If the testbench and the DUT used the same edge, the result would depend on the order in which the simulator runs the processes, and Icarus Verilog and Verilator choose this order differently.
The checks use !==, which also fails if the output is x, and end the simulation with $fatal(1, ...) on the first error. Do not use $error for this: Icarus Verilog only prints the message, reaches $finish, and exits with status 0, so a script or a make target cannot see that the test failed.
$dumpfile and $dumpvars write all signals into a waveform file in the Value Change Dump (VCD) format, and $finish ends the simulation.



2.6.2 A cocotb Testbench
cocotb (cocotb developers 2026) runs the testbench as Python code next to the simulator. Python then drives and reads the signals of the DUT through the programming interface of the simulator (the Verilog Procedural Interface, VPI, for Verilog simulators).


tick_gen/testbenches/cocotb/tick_gen_tb.py

# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Simon Dorrer
# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
# Description: Self-checking cocotb testbench for tick_gen.

import os
from pathlib import Path

import cocotb
from cocotb.clock import Clock
from cocotb.triggers import ClockCycles, FallingEdge
from cocotb_tools.runner import get_results, get_runner

DIV = 5  # passed to the DUT as parameter in the runner below


async def start_up(dut):
    """Start a 50 MHz clock and reset the DUT for two cycles."""
    cocotb.start_soon(Clock(dut.clk_i, 20, "ns").start())
    dut.rst_ni.value = 0
    dut.en_i.value = 0
    await ClockCycles(dut.clk_i, 2)
    await FallingEdge(dut.clk_i)
    dut.rst_ni.value = 1


@cocotb.test()
async def test_no_tick_when_disabled(dut):
    """tick_o stays low while en_i is low."""
    await start_up(dut)
    for _ in range(3 * DIV):
        await FallingEdge(dut.clk_i)
        assert dut.tick_o.value == 0, "tick while disabled"


@cocotb.test()
async def test_tick_every_div_cycles(dut):
    """tick_o is high for one cycle every DIV cycles."""
    await start_up(dut)
    dut.en_i.value = 1
    for cycle in range(1, 4 * DIV + 1):
        await FallingEdge(dut.clk_i)
        expected = 1 if cycle % DIV == 0 else 0
        assert dut.tick_o.value == expected, \
            f"cycle {cycle}: expected {expected}, got {dut.tick_o.value}"


def tick_gen_runner():
    sim = os.getenv("SIM", "icarus")
    proj_path = Path(__file__).resolve().parent

    runner = get_runner(sim)
    runner.build(
        sources=[proj_path / "../../rtl/tick_gen.sv"],
        hdl_toplevel="tick_gen",
        parameters={"DIV": DIV},
        always=True,
        waves=True,
        timescale=("1ns", "1ps"),
    )
    results_xml = runner.test(
        hdl_toplevel="tick_gen",
        test_module="tick_gen_tb",
        waves=True,
    )

    # A failing test leaves the exit status at 0, so check the results
    num_tests, num_failed = get_results(results_xml)
    if num_failed:
        raise SystemExit(
            f"FAIL: {num_failed} of {num_tests} tests failed")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    tick_gen_runner()



Every function decorated with @cocotb.test() is a test. The tests of a file run one after another in the same simulation, so each one starts its own clock and applies the reset.
Tests are coroutines (async def), which wait for simulator events with await: RisingEdge(sig), FallingEdge(sig), ClockCycles(sig, n), or Timer(t, "ns"). As in the SystemVerilog testbench, inputs are driven and outputs are checked on the falling edge.
dut.en_i.value = 1 writes an input, and dut.tick_o.value reads an output. A write takes effect at the end of the current time step, so reading the same signal right after writing it still returns the old value.
cocotb.start_soon(Clock(dut.clk_i, 20, "ns").start()) starts a 50 MHz clock that runs in parallel with the test.
A failing Python assert fails the test, and the f-string message explains why.
The function tick_gen_runner() follows the idiom of the AMS chip template: the file runs itself. It selects the simulator from the environment variable SIM (Icarus Verilog by default), builds the DUT with the given parameters, and runs the tests. runner.test() returns the path of the result file results.xml, but a failing test does not change the exit status of python3. The last lines therefore check the results with get_results() and exit with an error if any test failed.



2.6.3 SystemVerilog or cocotb?
Table 16 compares the two kinds of testbenches.



Table 16: SystemVerilog and cocotb testbenches










Aspect
SystemVerilog testbench
cocotb testbench




Language
SystemVerilog (the full language, including the simulation subset)
Python 3


Reference models
written in SystemVerilog
any Python code and library (e.g., NumPy)


Simulators
every SystemVerilog simulator
Icarus Verilog, Verilator, GHDL, and commercial simulators


DUT languages
SystemVerilog, VHDL only with a mixed-language simulator
the same testbench works for VHDL and SystemVerilog DUTs


Speed
fast, everything runs in the simulator
slower, every interaction passes through Python


In the AMS chip template
testbenches/verilog/
testbenches/cocotb/






In this course, we use both: a SystemVerilog testbench for a quick self-check of a block, and cocotb for everything that needs a reference model or randomized stimuli.

title: VLSI Design
section: 2.7 Linting, Simulation, and Synthesis in the IIC-OSIC-TOOLS Container
text:
2.7 Linting, Simulation, and Synthesis in the IIC-OSIC-TOOLS Container
All tools you need are installed in the IIC-OSIC-TOOLS container (Section 1.9). In the AMS chip template, they are wrapped in make targets. In this chapter, you type the commands yourself, so that you know what is behind the targets when you use them later (Section 2.8).

2.7.1 Setting Up a Working Folder
Start the container (Section 1.13) and open a terminal on its desktop. Create a folder for the tick generator with the same structure as a macro of the AMS chip template:
mkdir -p /foss/designs/sv_exercises/tick_gen/{rtl,testbenches/verilog,testbenches/cocotb}
cd /foss/designs/sv_exercises/tick_gen
Save the three listings as rtl/tick_gen.sv, testbenches/verilog/tick_gen_tb.sv, and testbenches/cocotb/tick_gen_tb.py, e.g., with gedit, vim, or VS Code. With a local installation, /foss/designs is the folder ~/eda/designs on your laptop, so your files survive when the container is removed or updated. All commands of this section start in the folder /foss/designs/sv_exercises/tick_gen.


2.7.2 Linting with Verilator
A linter checks the code for errors and suspicious constructs without simulating it. Run it first, on every RTL file, after every change:
verilator --lint-only -Wall rtl/tick_gen.sv
--lint-only only parses and checks the code, and -Wall enables all warnings, including the style warnings. Without any warning, Verilator only prints a short report and exits with status 0. Otherwise, it prints the warnings with file, line, and a link to their description, and exits with an error. Table 17 lists the warnings you will meet most often.



Table 17: Frequent Verilator warnings










Warning
Meaning
Typical fix




IMPLICIT
an undeclared name, Verilog created a 1-bit wire
fix the typo, add `default_nettype none


UNDRIVEN, UNUSEDSIGNAL
a signal is never assigned or never read
connect it or remove it


WIDTHTRUNC, WIDTHEXPAND
the widths of operands or of an assignment do not match
size the literals, extend with {1'b0, x}, or cast with N'(x)


LATCH
a combinational block (always_comb or always @(*)) does not assign a variable on every path
default assignments first, complete case and else


CASEINCOMPLETE
a case does not cover all values
add the missing items or a default


BLKSEQ
a blocking assignment = in always_ff
use <= instead


MULTIDRIVEN
a variable is driven from more than one block
assign it in exactly one block


DECLFILENAME
the file name differs from the module name
one module per file, with the same name






If a warning is a false alarm, you can switch it off for a few lines with /* verilator lint_off WIDTHEXPAND */ and /* verilator lint_on WIDTHEXPAND */, together with a comment that explains why. Never switch off warnings globally.


2.7.3 Simulating a SystemVerilog Testbench
Icarus Verilog compiles the design and the testbench into a simulation file, which vvp then runs:
iverilog -g2012 -o testbenches/verilog/tick_gen_tb.vvp \
  rtl/tick_gen.sv testbenches/verilog/tick_gen_tb.sv
cd testbenches/verilog
vvp tick_gen_tb.vvp
cd ../..
-g2012 selects the SystemVerilog standard IEEE 1800-2012, and -o names the output file. List the files in compile order: packages and files with `define macros first, then the modules. vvp writes the VCD file into the current folder, which is why we change into the testbench folder first and return afterwards. The simulation prints PASS: tick_gen_tb and exits with status 0, or stops at the first failed check with FATAL and exit status 1 (check it with echo $?).
Verilator can also run SystemVerilog testbenches. It compiles them into a C++ program, which is much faster for large designs. --binary builds an executable, and --timing enables the delays and event controls of the testbench. --timescale gives the RTL, which has no `timescale of its own, the same time unit as the testbench, and --trace enables the VCD output:
verilator --binary --timing --timescale 1ns/1ps --trace \
  --top-module tick_gen_tb -o tick_gen_tb \
  rtl/tick_gen.sv testbenches/verilog/tick_gen_tb.sv
cd testbenches/verilog
../../obj_dir/tick_gen_tb
cd ../..


2.7.4 Running a cocotb Testbench
A cocotb testbench in the template idiom runs itself:
cd testbenches/cocotb
python3 tick_gen_tb.py                  # with Icarus Verilog (default)
SIM=verilator python3 tick_gen_tb.py    # with Verilator
cd ../..
cocotb builds the simulation in the folder sim_build/, runs all tests, and prints a summary table with one line per test and a final line such as TESTS=2 PASS=2 FAIL=0 SKIP=0. The results are also stored in sim_build/results.xml. With Icarus Verilog, the waveform is written to sim_build/tick_gen.fst, with Verilator to sim_build/dump.vcd.


2.7.5 Viewing Waveforms
Open a waveform with GTKWave or Surfer:
gtkwave testbenches/verilog/tick_gen_tb.vcd
surfer testbenches/cocotb/sim_build/tick_gen.fst
In GTKWave, select a module in the hierarchy on the left, append its signals to the wave window, and zoom to fit. GTKWave can store the selected signals in a save file (.gtkw), which you pass as a second argument the next time, e.g., gtkwave tick_gen_tb.vcd tick_gen_tb.gtkw in the testbench folder. The AMS chip template keeps such save files next to its testbenches.


2.7.6 A Quick Synthesis Check with Yosys
A simulation shows what a design does, but not which hardware it becomes. A quick synthesis with Yosys answers this in a second:
yosys -p "read_verilog -sv rtl/tick_gen.sv; synth -top tick_gen; stat"
read_verilog -sv reads the file with the SystemVerilog front end, synth -top tick_gen synthesizes the design with tick_gen as top module onto generic gates, and stat prints the cell statistics at the end of the log. Check that the number of flip-flops ($_DFF_* and $_DFFE_* cells) matches the registers you intended and that there are no latches ($_DLATCH_* cells). The letters of a flip-flop name give the clock edge, the reset polarity, the reset value, and the enable polarity: $_DFFE_PN0P_ is a flip-flop on the positive clock edge (P) with an active-low reset (N) to zero (0) and an active-high enable (P). In the LibreLane flow, Yosys maps these generic cells onto the standard cells of SG13CMOS5L (Section 5).






TipExercise: Lint, Simulate, and Synthesize the Tick Generator




Set up the folder as described in Section 2.7.1 and save the three listings of the tick generator.
Lint the RTL with Verilator.
Run the SystemVerilog testbench with Icarus Verilog and look at the waveform in GTKWave. Find the cycles in which tick is high and compare them with count_q inside the DUT.
Run the cocotb testbench with Icarus Verilog and with Verilator, and open the cocotb waveform in Surfer.
Synthesize the RTL with Yosys. How many cells and flip-flops does it need, and of which types are the flip-flops?
Change DIV to 8 in both testbenches and rerun them. Since 8 is a power of two, the 3-bit counter uses all eight of its values. Then build in a bug: compare count_q with COUNT_LAST - 1 instead of COUNT_LAST. Do both testbenches catch it?



Before continuing, please finish the previous exercise. Once you are done, compare with the solution below.






TipSolution: Lint, Simulate, and Synthesize the Tick Generator






Verilator reports no warning.
The simulation prints PASS: tick_gen_tb. With DIV = 5, tick is high in the clock cycle after count_q has reached 4, i.e., once every five cycles while en is high.
Both runs end with TESTS=2 PASS=2 FAIL=0 SKIP=0. Icarus Verilog writes sim_build/tick_gen.fst, Verilator sim_build/dump.vcd.
With the default DIV = 10, Yosys 0.70 reports 17 cells, among them five flip-flops: four $_DFFE_PN0P_ cells for count_q (with an active-high enable input, which comes from en_i) and one $_DFF_PN0_ cell for tick_q.
With DIV = 8, both testbenches pass. With the bug, the counter wraps one cycle early, and both testbenches fail: the SystemVerilog testbench stops with FATAL and exit status 1, cocotb reports FAIL for test_tick_every_div_cycles, and the runner exits with an error.










TipExercise: PWM Generator with a SystemVerilog Testbench



Design a pulse-width modulation (PWM) generator pwm in the two-process style with these properties:

A parameter WIDTH (default 8) and the ports clk_i, rst_ni (asynchronous, active low), duty_i (WIDTH bits), and pwm_o.
An internal counter counts from 0 to \(2^\mathrm{WIDTH}-1\) and wraps around, so one PWM period lasts \(2^\mathrm{WIDTH}\) clock cycles.
In every period, pwm_o is high for exactly duty_i clock cycles. duty_i = 0 keeps the output low, and the maximum duty cycle is \((2^\mathrm{WIDTH}-1)/2^\mathrm{WIDTH}\).
pwm_o comes directly from a flip-flop, so that it has no glitches on its way to a pad.


Write the RTL in pwm/rtl/pwm.sv and lint it.
Write a self-checking SystemVerilog testbench pwm/testbenches/verilog/pwm_tb.sv with WIDTH = 4. For every one of the 16 duty values, it counts the high cycles of pwm_o within one period and stops with $fatal if the count is wrong. Also check that pwm_o is never x.
Run the testbench with Icarus Verilog and inspect the waveform.



Before continuing, please finish the previous exercise. Once you are done, compare with the solution below.






TipSolution: PWM Generator with a SystemVerilog Testbench







pwm/rtl/pwm.sv

// SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Simon Dorrer
// SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
// Description: PWM generator. In every period of 2**WIDTH clock
// cycles, pwm_o is high for exactly duty_i cycles (duty_i = 0 keeps
// it low).

`default_nettype none

module pwm #(
  parameter int unsigned WIDTH = 8
) (
  input  logic             clk_i,
  input  logic             rst_ni,
  input  logic [WIDTH-1:0] duty_i,
  output logic             pwm_o
);

  logic [WIDTH-1:0] count_d, count_q;
  logic             pwm_d, pwm_q;

  always_ff @(posedge clk_i or negedge rst_ni) begin
    if (!rst_ni) begin
      count_q <= '0;
      pwm_q   <= 1'b0;
    end else begin
      count_q <= count_d;
      pwm_q   <= pwm_d;
    end
  end

  always_comb begin
    count_d = count_q + 1'b1;  // wraps from 2**WIDTH - 1 to 0
    pwm_d   = (count_q < duty_i);
  end

  // Registered output: no glitches on the way to a pad
  assign pwm_o = pwm_q;

endmodule

`default_nettype wire


Since the counter has exactly WIDTH bits, it wraps around without any compare logic. The output register delays pwm_o by one cycle with respect to the comparison, which does not change the number of high cycles per period.


pwm/testbenches/verilog/pwm_tb.sv

// SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Simon Dorrer
// SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
// Description: Self-checking SystemVerilog testbench for pwm,
// testing all duty values of a 4-bit PWM.

`timescale 1ns / 1ps

module pwm_tb;

  localparam int unsigned WIDTH         = 4;
  localparam int unsigned PERIOD        = 2 ** WIDTH;
  localparam real         CLK_PERIOD_NS = 20.0;  // 50 MHz

  logic             clk   = 1'b0;
  logic             rst_n = 1'b0;
  logic [WIDTH-1:0] duty  = '0;
  logic             pwm_out;
  int unsigned      high_cycles;

  pwm #(
    .WIDTH(WIDTH)
  ) dut (
    .clk_i (clk),
    .rst_ni(rst_n),
    .duty_i(duty),
    .pwm_o (pwm_out)
  );

  always #(CLK_PERIOD_NS / 2) clk = ~clk;

  initial begin
    $dumpfile("pwm_tb.vcd");
    $dumpvars(0, pwm_tb);

    repeat (2) @(negedge clk);
    rst_n = 1'b1;

    for (int d = 0; d < PERIOD; d++) begin
      duty = WIDTH'(d);
      repeat (2) @(negedge clk);  // the new duty reaches pwm_o

      // Any PERIOD consecutive cycles contain exactly d high cycles
      high_cycles = 0;
      repeat (PERIOD) begin
        @(negedge clk);
        if ($isunknown(pwm_out)) $fatal(1, "FAIL: pwm_o is X or Z");
        if (pwm_out) high_cycles++;
      end
      if (high_cycles != d) begin
        $fatal(1, "FAIL: duty %0d gives %0d high cycles", d,
               high_cycles);
      end
    end

    $display("PASS: pwm_tb");
    $finish;
  end

endmodule


After a new duty value is applied, the testbench waits two cycles until it has reached the output register. Then any \(2^\mathrm{WIDTH}\) consecutive cycles contain exactly duty high cycles, regardless of where the period starts, so the testbench does not need to know the internal counter. $isunknown() is true if any bit is x or z. The commands are:
cd /foss/designs/sv_exercises/pwm
verilator --lint-only -Wall rtl/pwm.sv
iverilog -g2012 -o testbenches/verilog/pwm_tb.vvp rtl/pwm.sv testbenches/verilog/pwm_tb.sv
cd testbenches/verilog && vvp pwm_tb.vvp
gtkwave pwm_tb.vcd
To check that the testbench really checks something, change < to <= in the comparison: the testbench then stops with FATAL and the message FAIL: duty 0 gives 1 high cycles.









TipExercise: PWM Generator with a cocotb Testbench



Write a cocotb testbench pwm/testbenches/cocotb/pwm_tb.py for your PWM generator from the previous exercise, again with WIDTH = 4:

A test test_all_duty_values with the same check as the SystemVerilog testbench. In cocotb, dut.pwm_o.value.is_resolvable is false if any bit is x or z, so not dut.pwm_o.value.is_resolvable corresponds to $isunknown().
A test test_against_model that changes duty_i to random values at random times (use a fixed seed, e.g., random.Random(42)) and compares pwm_o in every clock cycle with a cycle-accurate Python model of the counter and the output register.
A runner in the template idiom of Section 2.6.2, which exits with an error if a test fails.

Run the testbench with Icarus Verilog and with Verilator.


Before continuing, please finish the previous exercise. Once you are done, compare with the solution below.






TipSolution: PWM Generator with a cocotb Testbench







pwm/testbenches/cocotb/pwm_tb.py

# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Simon Dorrer
# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
# Description: Self-checking cocotb testbench for pwm (4-bit PWM).

import os
import random
from pathlib import Path

import cocotb
from cocotb.clock import Clock
from cocotb.triggers import ClockCycles, FallingEdge
from cocotb_tools.runner import get_results, get_runner

WIDTH = 4
PERIOD = 2**WIDTH


async def start_up(dut):
    """Start a 50 MHz clock and reset the DUT for two cycles."""
    cocotb.start_soon(Clock(dut.clk_i, 20, "ns").start())
    dut.rst_ni.value = 0
    dut.duty_i.value = 0
    await ClockCycles(dut.clk_i, 2)
    await FallingEdge(dut.clk_i)
    dut.rst_ni.value = 1


@cocotb.test()
async def test_all_duty_values(dut):
    """For every duty d, pwm_o is high for d cycles per period."""
    await start_up(dut)
    for duty in range(PERIOD):
        dut.duty_i.value = duty
        for _ in range(2):  # the new duty reaches pwm_o
            await FallingEdge(dut.clk_i)
        high_cycles = 0
        for _ in range(PERIOD):
            await FallingEdge(dut.clk_i)
            assert dut.pwm_o.value.is_resolvable, "pwm_o is X or Z"
            high_cycles += int(dut.pwm_o.value)
        assert high_cycles == duty, \
            f"duty {duty} gives {high_cycles} high cycles"


@cocotb.test()
async def test_against_model(dut):
    """Random duty changes, checked cycle by cycle against a model."""
    await start_up(dut)
    rng = random.Random(42)  # fixed seed: every run is reproducible
    count, pwm, duty = 0, 0, 0  # model state after reset
    for _ in range(20 * PERIOD):
        if rng.random() < 0.05:
            # Keep the value in Python: a write becomes visible in
            # the DUT only at the end of the current time step
            duty = rng.randrange(PERIOD)
            dut.duty_i.value = duty
        await FallingEdge(dut.clk_i)
        # Model of the rising edge: both registers update at once
        pwm = 1 if count < duty else 0
        count = (count + 1) % PERIOD
        assert dut.pwm_o.value == pwm, \
            f"expected {pwm}, got {dut.pwm_o.value}"


def pwm_runner():
    sim = os.getenv("SIM", "icarus")
    proj_path = Path(__file__).resolve().parent

    runner = get_runner(sim)
    runner.build(
        sources=[proj_path / "../../rtl/pwm.sv"],
        hdl_toplevel="pwm",
        parameters={"WIDTH": WIDTH},
        always=True,
        waves=True,
        timescale=("1ns", "1ps"),
    )
    results_xml = runner.test(
        hdl_toplevel="pwm",
        test_module="pwm_tb",
        waves=True,
    )

    # A failing test leaves the exit status at 0, so check the results
    num_tests, num_failed = get_results(results_xml)
    if num_failed:
        raise SystemExit(
            f"FAIL: {num_failed} of {num_tests} tests failed")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    pwm_runner()


The model in test_against_model mirrors the two registers of the DUT: at every rising edge, the new pwm value is computed from the old counter value, and the counter increments, exactly like the two non-blocking assignments in always_ff. The comment on duty explains why the model keeps its own copy of the value it writes. Reading dut.duty_i.value right after the write would still return the old value, and the model would be one cycle off. Both simulators report TESTS=2 PASS=2 FAIL=0 SKIP=0. The model test is the stronger one: a counter that wraps at 14 instead of 15 fails both tests, but only the model test would also find a bug that keeps the number of high cycles right and shifts the pulse within the period.









TipExercise: Sequence Detector FSM



The following VHDL FSM detects the bit pattern 1011 in a serial input. It samples one bit at each rising clock edge, and overlapping occurrences count, so 1011011 contains the pattern twice. detect_o is high for one clock cycle after the edge that sampled the last 1 of the pattern (Moore output).


seq_detect/vhdl/seq_detect_ea.vhd

-- SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Simon Dorrer
-- SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
-- Description: Moore FSM that detects the bit pattern 1011 in the
-- serial input bit_i (one bit per rising clock edge, overlapping
-- occurrences count). detect_o is high for one cycle after the edge
-- that sampled the last 1.

library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;

entity seq_detect is
  port(
    clk_i    : in  std_logic;
    rst_i    : in  std_logic;
    bit_i    : in  std_logic;
    detect_o : out std_logic
  );
end entity seq_detect;

architecture rtl of seq_detect is
  -- Each state names the longest matched prefix of 1011
  type t_state is (DET_IDLE, DET_1, DET_10, DET_101, DET_1011);

  signal state      : t_state;
  signal next_state : t_state;
begin
  reg_proc: process(rst_i, clk_i) is
  begin
    if rst_i = '1' then
      state <= DET_IDLE;
    elsif rising_edge(clk_i) then
      state <= next_state;
    end if;
  end process reg_proc;

  fsm_logic: process(state, bit_i) is
  begin
    next_state <= state;
    detect_o <= '0';
    case state is
      when DET_IDLE =>
        if bit_i = '1' then
          next_state <= DET_1;
        end if;
      when DET_1 =>
        if bit_i = '0' then
          next_state <= DET_10;
        end if;
      when DET_10 =>
        if bit_i = '1' then
          next_state <= DET_101;
        else
          next_state <= DET_IDLE;
        end if;
      when DET_101 =>
        if bit_i = '1' then
          next_state <= DET_1011;
        else
          next_state <= DET_10;
        end if;
      when DET_1011 =>
        detect_o <= '1';
        if bit_i = '1' then
          next_state <= DET_1;
        else
          next_state <= DET_10;
        end if;
    end case;
  end process fsm_logic;
end architecture rtl;



Draw the state diagram.
Translate the FSM into a SystemVerilog module seq_detect in seq_detect/rtl/seq_detect.sv, with an asynchronous active-low reset rst_ni instead of rst_i and otherwise the same port names, which the testbench below uses. Lint it.
Verify it with the following cocotb testbench, which compares detect_o with a Python reference model for a directed and a random bit stream. Run it with Icarus Verilog and with Verilator.



seq_detect/testbenches/cocotb/seq_detect_tb.py

# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Simon Dorrer
# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
# Description: Self-checking cocotb testbench for seq_detect with a
# Python reference model.

import os
import random
from pathlib import Path

import cocotb
from cocotb.clock import Clock
from cocotb.triggers import ClockCycles, FallingEdge
from cocotb_tools.runner import get_results, get_runner

PATTERN = [1, 0, 1, 1]


async def start_up(dut):
    """Start a 50 MHz clock and reset the DUT for two cycles."""
    cocotb.start_soon(Clock(dut.clk_i, 20, "ns").start())
    dut.rst_ni.value = 0
    dut.bit_i.value = 0
    await ClockCycles(dut.clk_i, 2)
    await FallingEdge(dut.clk_i)
    dut.rst_ni.value = 1


async def send_and_check(dut, bits):
    """Send one bit per cycle, compare detect_o with the model."""
    history = []
    detections = 0
    for bit in bits:
        dut.bit_i.value = bit
        # The DUT samples the bit at the rising edge in between
        await FallingEdge(dut.clk_i)
        history.append(bit)
        expected = 1 if history[-len(PATTERN):] == PATTERN else 0
        assert dut.detect_o.value == expected, \
            f"after bits ...{history[-8:]}: " \
            f"expected {expected}, got {dut.detect_o.value}"
        detections += expected
    return detections


@cocotb.test()
async def test_overlapping(dut):
    """1011011 contains the pattern twice, the second overlapping."""
    await start_up(dut)
    detections = await send_and_check(dut, [1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0])
    assert detections == 2, f"expected 2 detections, got {detections}"


@cocotb.test()
async def test_random_bits(dut):
    """A long random bit stream against the reference model."""
    await start_up(dut)
    rng = random.Random(1234)  # fixed seed: every run is reproducible
    bits = [rng.randint(0, 1) for _ in range(500)]
    detections = await send_and_check(dut, bits)
    # Guard against a test that passes without ever seeing the pattern
    assert detections > 0, "no pattern in the random stream"
    dut._log.info(f"{detections} detections in {len(bits)} bits")


def seq_detect_runner():
    sim = os.getenv("SIM", "icarus")
    proj_path = Path(__file__).resolve().parent

    runner = get_runner(sim)
    runner.build(
        sources=[proj_path / "../../rtl/seq_detect.sv"],
        hdl_toplevel="seq_detect",
        always=True,
        waves=True,
        timescale=("1ns", "1ps"),
    )
    results_xml = runner.test(
        hdl_toplevel="seq_detect",
        test_module="seq_detect_tb",
        waves=True,
    )

    # A failing test leaves the exit status at 0, so check the results
    num_tests, num_failed = get_results(results_xml)
    if num_failed:
        raise SystemExit(
            f"FAIL: {num_failed} of {num_tests} tests failed")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    seq_detect_runner()




Before continuing, please finish the previous exercise. Once you are done, compare with the solution below.






TipSolution: Sequence Detector FSM





Each state stores the longest prefix of 1011 that the received bits end with. A 0 after 1011 leaves 10, and a 1 leaves 1, which is how overlapping occurrences are detected. Table 18 gives the state diagram as a table, with the state names of the VHDL version. In the SystemVerilog solution, DET_IDLE becomes StIdle, DET_1 becomes St1, and so on.

// SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Simon Dorrer
// SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
// Description: Moore FSM that detects the bit pattern 1011 in the
// serial input bit_i (one bit per rising clock edge, overlapping
// occurrences count). detect_o is high for one cycle after the edge
// that sampled the last 1.

`default_nettype none

module seq_detect (
  input  logic clk_i,
  input  logic rst_ni,
  input  logic bit_i,
  output logic detect_o
);

  // Each state names the longest matched prefix of 1011
  typedef enum logic [2:0] {
    StIdle,
    St1,
    St10,
    St101,
    St1011
  } state_e;

  state_e state_d, state_q;

  always_ff @(posedge clk_i or negedge rst_ni) begin
    if (!rst_ni) begin
      state_q <= StIdle;
    end else begin
      state_q <= state_d;
    end
  end

  always_comb begin
    state_d  = state_q;
    detect_o = 1'b0;
    unique case (state_q)
      StIdle: begin
        if (bit_i) state_d = St1;
      end
      St1: begin
        if (!bit_i) state_d = St10;
      end
      St10: begin
        if (bit_i) state_d = St101;
        else       state_d = StIdle;
      end
      St101: begin
        if (bit_i) state_d = St1011;
        else       state_d = St10;
      end
      St1011: begin
        detect_o = 1'b1;
        if (bit_i) state_d = St1;
        else       state_d = St10;
      end
      default: state_d = StIdle;  // unused encodings
    endcase
  end

endmodule

`default_nettype wire


Five states need a 3-bit encoding, so three encodings are unused, and the default item sends them back to idle. Both simulators report TESTS=2 PASS=2 FAIL=0 SKIP=0, and the random stream of 500 bits contains the pattern 31 times. The testbench checks that this count is not zero, so that the random test cannot pass without ever seeing the pattern. Icarus Verilog prints a “sorry” message that it ignores unique, which you can disregard. Since cocotb is independent of the HDL, the same testbench also runs the VHDL version with GHDL (with the active-high reset rst_i instead of rst_ni), and both versions pass.

section: 2.8 Hands-On: The Counter of the AMS Chip Template
text:
2.8 Hands-On: The Counter of the AMS Chip Template
In this course, you use the SG13CMOS5L version of the AMS chip template, ihp-sg13cmos5l-ams-chip-template, together with its tutorial. Its digital example is the macro macros/counter: an 8-bit counter with a synchronous reset, an enable, and a wrap-around at CTR_MAX, plus a wrapper counter_top, which converts the active-low reset of the chip into the active-high reset of the counter. The tutorial shows the complete code of the counter in its section counter.sv. The macro comes with a SystemVerilog and a cocotb testbench, and its Makefile wraps the commands of Section 2.7 into make targets. In the following exercises, you first type the commands yourself and only then look at the targets.






TipExercise: Lint and Simulate the Counter by Hand



Clone the template into your designs folder (if you have not done so yet) and change into the counter macro:
cd /foss/designs
git clone https://github.com/iic-jku/ihp-sg13cmos5l-ams-chip-template.git
cd ihp-sg13cmos5l-ams-chip-template/macros/counter

Read rtl/constants.sv, rtl/counter.sv, and rtl/counter_top.sv.
Lint counter_top together with the files it needs with verilator --lint-only -Wall. In which order do you have to pass the files, and why?
Compile the SystemVerilog testbench testbenches/verilog/counter_top_tb.sv with Icarus Verilog, run it in its folder, and open the waveform with the saved signal list counter_top_tb.gtkw.
Run the cocotb testbench testbenches/cocotb/counter_top_tb.py with the default simulator and open its waveform.
The counter has four behaviors: reset, hold while disabled, increment while enabled, and wrap-around at CTR_MAX. Which of them does each testbench actually check?



Before continuing, please finish the previous exercise. Once you are done, compare with the solution below.






TipSolution: Lint and Simulate the Counter by Hand





# Lint (no warning, even with -Wall)
verilator --lint-only -Wall rtl/constants.sv rtl/counter.sv rtl/counter_top.sv

# SystemVerilog testbench with Icarus Verilog
iverilog -g2012 -o testbenches/verilog/counter_top_tb.vvp \
  rtl/constants.sv rtl/counter.sv rtl/counter_top.sv \
  testbenches/verilog/counter_top_tb.sv
cd testbenches/verilog
vvp counter_top_tb.vvp
gtkwave counter_top_tb.vcd counter_top_tb.gtkw

# cocotb testbench
cd ../cocotb
python3 counter_top_tb.py
gtkwave sim_build/counter_top.fst counter_top_tb.gtkw

constants.sv defines the macros `COUNTER_MAX_DEFAULT and `CLK_FREQ_DEFAULT, which counter_top.sv and the testbench use. A macro must be defined before it is used, and the tools read the files in the given order, so constants.sv comes first.
The SystemVerilog testbench prints PASS: simulation complete., and the cocotb testbench reports TESTS=4 PASS=4 FAIL=0 SKIP=0.
The cocotb testbench checks all four behaviors, one test each. The SystemVerilog testbench (template version of October 2026) checks only two: the counter is zero after the reset, and it stays zero while disabled. It enables the counter for a full wrap-around, but does not check the values, so increment and wrap-around are only visible in the waveform. A PASS only means that the implemented checks passed.










TipExercise: The Counter in the Two-Process Style




Draw the counter as a synchronous sequential circuit in the structure of Figure 4. Which signal is the state, which are the inputs, and which operations does the next-state logic need?
Turn your diagram into the two-process style: rewrite rtl/counter.sv with count_d and count_q, the register in always_ff and the next-state logic in always_comb. Keep the module name, the parameters, the ports, and the behavior (synchronous reset, enable, wrap-around at CTR_MAX) exactly as they are.
Lint the design and run both testbenches again. All checks must still pass, which shows that your refactoring did not change the checked behavior.
Now build in a bug: let the counter wrap one value early (compare with CTR_MAX - 1). Run both testbenches again and check their exit status with echo $?. Which testbench finds the bug? What does the exit status tell you?
Restore the original file with git restore rtl/counter.sv.



Before continuing, please finish the previous exercise. Once you are done, compare with the solution below.






TipSolution: The Counter in the Two-Process Style





Figure 9 shows the counter in the structure of Figure 4. The state is count_q, held in CTR_BW flip-flops with the clock clock_i and the synchronous reset reset_i. The next-state logic gets count_q and the input enable_i and needs four parts: a comparator with CTR_MAX, an incrementer, a first multiplexer that selects zero at the wrap-around, and a second multiplexer that keeps count_q while enable_i is low.








Figure 9: The counter of the AMS chip template as register and next-state logic, in the structure of Figure 4. The register holds count_q and has the synchronous reset reset_i. In the next-state logic, the comparator and the incrementer work on count_q in parallel, the first multiplexer selects zero at the wrap-around, and the second keeps count_q while enable_i is low.





In the code, the register becomes always_ff, and the next-state logic becomes always_comb, where the two multiplexers turn into the if and else decisions:


macros/counter/rtl/counter.sv (two-process version)

// SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Simon Dorrer and Harald Pretl
// SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0 WITH SHL-2.1
// Description: This file implements an N-bit up counter with
// synchronous reset & enable in SystemVerilog (two-process style).

`default_nettype none
`ifndef __COUNTER__
`define __COUNTER__

module counter #(
  parameter int unsigned       CTR_BW  = 8,
  parameter logic [CTR_BW-1:0] CTR_MAX = 2**CTR_BW - 1
)(
  input logic               clock_i,
  input logic               reset_i,
  input logic               enable_i,

  output logic [CTR_BW-1:0] counter_value_o
);

  logic [CTR_BW-1:0] count_d, count_q;

  // Register process: synchronous reset and copy of count_d only
  always_ff @(posedge clock_i) begin
    if (reset_i) begin
      count_q <= '0;
    end else begin
      count_q <= count_d;
    end
  end

  // Combinational process: next counter value, wraps around at CTR_MAX
  always_comb begin
    count_d = count_q;
    if (enable_i) begin
      if (count_q == CTR_MAX) begin
        count_d = '0;
      end else begin
        count_d = count_q + 1'b1;
      end
    end
  end

  assign counter_value_o = count_q;

endmodule // counter

`endif
`default_nettype wire


The synchronous reset stays in the register process, so always_ff holds the reset value and the copy of count_d, as in your VHDL reg_proc. Putting the reset into the combinational process as the first decision would describe the same hardware. Lint and both testbenches pass as before.
With the bug, the SystemVerilog testbench still prints PASS and exits with status 0, because it does not check the wrap-around. In the cocotb testbench, test_wraps_at_max fails, but python3 counter_top_tb.py still exits with status 0, because the runner of the template does not evaluate results.xml (compare it with the runner of Section 2.6.2). Two lessons follow: a testbench is only as good as its checks, and an exit status is only useful if the script sets it. Both matter as soon as testbenches run automatically, e.g., in a regression with make or in continuous integration.









TipExercise: What Is Behind the Make Targets?



Open macros/counter/Makefile of the template.

make help lists all targets. Try it, then try make -n sim-rtl-verilog, which prints the commands of a target without running them (dry run). What does the Makefile check before it runs a target, and what do you have to do if this check fails?
Find the targets that run the commands you typed in the previous exercises, and compare their commands (make -n <target>) with yours. What is different?



Before continuing, please finish the previous exercise. Once you are done, compare with the solution below.






TipSolution: What Is Behind the Make Targets?





Every target except help and clean first checks that the environment variable PDK is ihp-sg13cmos5l, because the macro is built for this PDK. If the shell is set to another PDK (the default of the container is ihp-sg13g2, check it with echo $PDK), the Makefile stops with an error message, even for a dry run. Switch the PDK with sak-pdk ihp-sg13cmos5l in the same shell and try again. Your own commands did not need this, because an RTL simulation does not use the PDK. Table 19 compares the targets with your commands.

Your command
Make target
Differences




verilator --lint-only -Wall ...
make lint-verilog, make lint-verilog CELL=counter, make lint-verilog-all (both)
without -Wall, with the include path -I"rtl", CELL selects the files

After the switch, make -n sim-rtl-verilog prints:
iverilog -g2012 -DSIM -o testbenches/verilog/test_counter_top \
  rtl/constants.sv rtl/counter.sv rtl/counter_top.sv \
  testbenches/verilog/counter_top_tb.sv
cd testbenches/verilog && vvp test_counter_top
rm -f testbenches/verilog/test_counter_top
The variable CELL (default counter_top) selects the cell, e.g., make lint-verilog CELL=counter. From now on, you can use the make targets, knowing what they do.

title: VLSI Design
text:
2.9 HDL Coding Guidelines

“A consistent naming and schematic drawing style, as well as VHDL/Verilog coding scheme, is a huge help in avoiding errors and increasing productivity.” (Circuit Designer’s Etiquette)

The VHDL/Verilog Coding Guide of the Circuit Designer’s Etiquette was written for Verilog and applies to SystemVerilog with small adaptations. Its rules, restated for the SystemVerilog of this course:

Lint every file with verilator --lint-only -Wall and fix every warning. A warning you ignore today hides the one that matters tomorrow.
Write readable code with descriptive names and comments that explain the intention. Inputs end in _i, outputs in _o, bidirectional ports in _io. An active-low signal has an n before the direction suffix, e.g., rst_ni.
Choose the reset deliberately. A synchronous reset avoids reset races. An asynchronous reset, our default, must be free of glitches and released synchronously (Section 8).
Use logic for all signals. The suffixes _w and _r of plain Verilog for wire and reg are not needed.
Use assign for simple logic. The conditional operator c ? a : b is often clearer than a nested if.
Declare every port explicitly with direction, type, and width (output logic [7:0] data_o).
Use localparam for constants and write parameters in UPPERCASE.
Reset every register that holds control state, e.g., FSM states, counters, and valid flags, to a defined value.
One module per file, and the file name equals the module name.
Start every file with `default_nettype none and end it with `default_nettype wire, as a safety net against typos.
Use always_comb for combinational logic. It replaces the always @(*) of plain Verilog and never has an incomplete sensitivity list.
Parameterize bit widths and other values with parameters and localparams.
Make conversions and widths explicit instead of relying on implicit extension and truncation (Section 2.5.3).
Use blocking assignments = only in always_comb and non-blocking assignments <= only in always_ff.
Make visible whether a control acts synchronously or asynchronously. The etiquette names synchronous set and reset set and res, and asynchronous ones pre (preset) and clr (clear). In this course, the asynchronous reset of a block is rst_ni, and a synchronous reset or clear is an ordinary input, such as reset_i in the counter of the AMS chip template.

From the lowRISC style guide (lowRISC 2026), we additionally adopt the suffixes _d and _q for the next and current value of a register, _e for enumeration types and _t for other types, UpperCamelCase state names, unique case with a default, named connections for every port and parameter, and no plain always blocks. For parameters, however, we keep the UPPERCASE names of the etiquette (rule 7), while lowRISC uses UpperCamelCase. Finally, Table 20 collects the traps that VHDL designers fall into most often.



Table 20: Pitfalls for VHDL designers

title: VLSI Design
text:
2.10 Summary

An HDL describes hardware that works concurrently, not instructions that run one after another. Think hardware first, then write the code.
Almost every digital circuit is a register plus combinational next-state logic. The register loads the next state at every rising clock edge, so the logic has one clock period to compute it.
Many HDLs exist, but all alternatives can generate (System)Verilog, which then runs through the same tools. SystemVerilog is the industry standard and the language of our open-source flow.
Your VHDL two-process style maps directly onto SystemVerilog: always_ff holds the reset values and copies _d into _q, and always_comb starts with defaults and contains all decisions.
Use logic, always_comb with =, always_ff with <=, sized literals, and an asynchronous active-low reset rst_ni. Lint every file and check it with a quick Yosys synthesis.
Plain Verilog is everywhere, in netlists, cell models, generated code, and older IP. Read it, but write SystemVerilog: logic instead of reg and wire, always_comb and always_ff instead of always.
Make every testbench self-checking, drive and check on the falling clock edge, and make sure that a failure sets the exit status: $fatal in SystemVerilog, get_results() in a cocotb runner.
The make targets of the AMS chip template wrap the commands you typed in this chapter, with small differences, e.g., -DSIM and no -Wall (Table 19).

In Section 3, we look at modeling guidelines that turn correct RTL into RTL that synthesizes well, and Section 4 takes the cocotb testbenches of this chapter to a systematic verification methodology.

title: VLSI Design
text:
3.1 Learning Objectives
After this chapter, you will be able to:

explain why the simulation of the RTL and of the synthesized netlist must agree, and name the typical causes of a mismatch
predict how if, case, and the conditional operator treat an unknown value x, in an RTL and in a gate-level simulation, and explain why Verilator shows no x at all
find a missing reset in simulation, and decide which registers need a reset
recognize FPGA habits that do not carry over to an ASIC, such as initial values, divided clocks, inferred block RAMs, and internal tri-state buses
replace a divided clock by a clock enable
design the boundary of a macro so that its timing is easy to close and the same testbench runs on the RTL and on the netlist
compare architectures of the same function by area and timing with Yosys and OpenSTA, and explain why the architecture matters more than the coding style

title: VLSI Design
text:
3.2 Simulation Must Match the Netlist
A hardware description exists at several levels of abstraction. A behavioral model describes the function only, e.g., a reference model in Python or a testbench that uses delays, files, and real numbers. The register-transfer level (RTL) describes the registers and the combinational logic between them (Section 2.2.2), and it is the level you write and synthesize. The gate level is a netlist of standard cells, the output of logic synthesis. Finally, the layout describes the polygons on the masks. The digital design flow (Section 1.8) translates the RTL into the netlist and the netlist into the layout.
Here lies a trap. You verify the RTL, but the chip implements the netlist. If both behave differently, all simulations of the RTL are worthless, and without further checks you only find out on the chip. Figure 10 shows the two ways to check that the netlist implements the RTL: a gate-level simulation of the netlist with the same testbench, and a logic equivalence check, which proves it without any simulation (Section 5).








Figure 10: You verify the RTL, but the chip implements the netlist. The same testbench drives the RTL simulation and the gate-level simulation of the synthesized netlist, and both must give the same results. Logic equivalence checking (Section 5) proves that the netlist implements the RTL without any simulation.





The two checks complement each other. The gate-level simulation only covers the stimuli of the testbench, but it shows what the netlist does from its real, unknown start state. The equivalence check covers every input sequence, but it works with the two values 0 and 1 and starts both designs from the same state, so it cannot see a mismatch that comes from unknown start values (Section 3.3.1). Neither of them tells you how to avoid a mismatch, and debugging a netlist is hard. It consists of thousands of cells with generated names, the FSM states have lost their names, and the hierarchy is flattened. In the final netlist of the counter of the AMS chip template, for example, the outputs of the eight flip-flops are called net3 to net10. It pays to write RTL that cannot cause a mismatch in the first place. Mismatches have only a few root causes:

Simulation semantics that synthesis ignores: the unknown value x and initial values. They are the subject of Section 3.3 and Section 3.4.1.
Constructs that tools read differently: incomplete sensitivity lists, the full_case and parallel_case pragmas, and unique case without default. Section 2 already showed how to avoid them (Section 2.5.5, Section 2.5.13).
Timing that the RTL simulation does not model: glitches of combinational outputs and the delay of a derived clock. Section 3.4.2 and Section 3.5 show how to design them away, and Section 6 covers timing in depth.

title: VLSI Design
text:
3.3 Four-Valued Simulation, Two-Valued Silicon
A variable of type logic has four values (Section 2.5.2): 0, 1, z for high impedance, and x for unknown. Silicon has only two: every node is either low or high, apart from short transitions. An x is the simulator’s way of saying that it does not know which of the two. The most common sources of x are a register without reset before its first load, a net with two conflicting drivers, an explicit assignment of 'x, and an array index out of range.
A perfect simulator would set a signal to x only if it could really be 0 or 1 in the hardware. Such an exact analysis is far too expensive, so the language defines simple rules for every operator and statement instead, and these rules err in both directions:

X-optimism: the simulation shows a known value where the hardware could have either. An if treats an unknown condition as false and takes the else branch, and a case item never matches an unknown expression, so the default branch runs.
X-pessimism: the simulation shows x where the hardware has a known value, e.g., because an x that cancels out in the hardware is still propagated.

The following testbench describes a 2:1 multiplexer in three ways, plus an AND gate, and sets the select sel to x. The default branch of the case assigns x only for this demonstration.


xprop/testbenches/verilog/xprop_tb.sv

// SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Simon Dorrer
// SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
// Description: Three ways to describe a 2:1 multiplexer, plus an AND
// gate, simulated with an unknown select. Shows how if, case, ?:, and
// & treat x.

`timescale 1ns / 1ps

module xprop_tb;

  logic sel, a, b;
  logic y_if, y_case, y_cond, y_and;

  always_comb begin
    if (sel) y_if = b;
    else     y_if = a;
  end

  always_comb begin
    case (sel)
      1'b0:    y_case = a;
      1'b1:    y_case = b;
      default: y_case = 1'bx;  // only for this demonstration
    endcase
  end

  assign y_cond = sel ? b : a;
  assign y_and  = sel & a;

  initial begin
    sel = 1'bx;
    {a, b} = 2'b01;
    #1 $display("sel=x a=0 b=1: if=%b case=%b ?:=%b and=%b",
                y_if, y_case, y_cond, y_and);
    {a, b} = 2'b11;
    #1 $display("sel=x a=1 b=1: if=%b case=%b ?:=%b and=%b",
                y_if, y_case, y_cond, y_and);
    $finish;
  end

endmodule

Five lessons follow from the table:

if is optimistic. With a=0 and b=1, it shows a clean 0 where the hardware could have either value. A bug that leaves a select unknown is invisible behind an if.
A default that assigns x is pessimistic. With a=b=1, the case shows x, although the hardware gives 1 for either select. With a defined default, as in the FSM of Section 3.3.1, the case is optimistic like the if.
The conditional operator ?: behaves like the multiplexer cell. For an unknown select, it merges both inputs bit by bit: equal bits stay known, different bits become x. A multiplexer that synthesis builds from AND and OR gates, however, is pessimistic again, since (x & 1) | (~x & 1) gives x. Even a gate-level simulation is only as exact as its cells.
The AND gate is exact. Icarus Verilog knows that x & 0 is 0.
Verilator knows no x. It is a two-state simulator and replaces every x by a two-state value, here 0, so its results are those of sel = 0. That makes Verilator fast, but it hides every unknown value. The option --x-assign selects what an explicit 'x becomes, by default the value that simulates fastest. The option --x-initial selects what the variables start with. With its default, unique, they start at 0, unless the run-time option +verilator+rand+reset+2 asks for random values, and +verilator+seed+<n> selects the seed. Random start values are what silicon does: every flip-flop powers up as 0 or 1, and nobody knows which.

Since an x cannot be trusted in either direction, the guidelines are strict. Never assign 'x in RTL. The lowRISC style guide puts it clearly: “The use of X literals in RTL code is strongly discouraged” (lowRISC 2026). An 'x tells the synthesis tool that it may choose any value, so the netlist can implement a value that the RTL simulation never showed. Assign a defined default instead, as the two-process style does (Section 2.5.7). Do not take the absence of x in an RTL simulation as a proof that a design is defined. Run the regression in Verilator with random start values and several seeds, and simulate the netlist at least once (Section 4). With --x-assign unique, Verilator also randomizes the explicit 'x assignments that slipped through. In testbench checks, compare with !== or $isunknown(), as in Table 20.

3.3.1 The Missing Reset
The most common source of an unknown value is a register without reset. As an example, take the controller FSM of Section 2.5.9 and remove the reset from its state register:
// State register without a reset: its start value is unknown
always_ff @(posedge clk_i) begin
  state_q <= state_d;
end
The complete module is ctrl_fsm_noreset/rtl/ctrl_fsm_noreset.sv. Its testbench prints the first eight clock cycles after power-up, with start_i high in cycle 2 and last_i high in cycle 4. Figure 11 compares four simulations of the same RTL: Icarus Verilog, Verilator with its default start values, Verilator with random start values, and Icarus Verilog with the netlist that Yosys synthesizes onto SG13CMOS5L cells.








Figure 11: The controller FSM of Section 2.5.9 without a reset, in the first eight clock cycles after power-up (start_i high in cycle 2, last_i in cycle 4). In the RTL simulation, the state starts unknown (hatched), but the default branch returns it to StIdle at the first clock edge, and the outputs never show x. Icarus Verilog and Verilator give the same outputs. The gate-level simulation of the synthesized netlist shows x until start_i forces a known state. With random start values, Verilator shows what the chip can do after power-up: a run that was never started (seed 3) or a done_o pulse for it (seed 9).






In the RTL simulation with Icarus Verilog, state_q starts as xx. No case item matches, so the default branch sets state_d to StIdle, and the outputs keep their default value 0. After the first clock edge, the FSM is in StIdle and works perfectly. The missing reset is invisible: the X-optimism of the case statement keeps every x away from the outputs.
Verilator starts state_q at 00, which is StIdle. The missing reset is invisible again.
With random start values, Verilator shows what the chip does after power-up. Seed 1 starts in StIdle (00) and seed 2 in the unused code 11, which the default branch turns into StIdle after one cycle. Both are harmless. Seed 3, however, starts in StRun (01): busy_o is high from cycle 0 until last_i ends a run that was never started. Seed 9 starts in StDone (10), and done_o reports the end of a job that never existed. Which of these a chip shows depends on the die, the supply ramp, and the temperature.
The gate-level simulation of the netlist shows that something is wrong: busy_o and done_o are x in cycle 0, and busy_o stays x until start_i forces a known state.

The guidelines for resets are therefore:

Reset every register that holds control state: FSM states, counters, valid flags, and pointers (Section 2.9, rule 8).
A data register may stay without reset if the control logic guarantees that it is written before it is read, e.g., a pipeline register behind a valid flag, or the content of a memory. Large designs often omit these resets, because the reset net must reach every flip-flop that uses it, and it then needs its own buffer tree and timing checks like a clock. In SG13CMOS5L, a register without reset saves no cell area, though: the library has no flip-flop without reset. Its flip-flops are dfrbp and dfrbpq and the scan flip-flops sdfrbp, sdfrbpq, and sdfbbp (Section 9), and all of them have a reset input, which synthesis simply ties inactive for a register without reset.
Use the four-state type logic for registers, also as the base type of an enumeration. The two-state types bit and int start at 0 in every simulator and hide a missing reset, just like Verilator. In VHDL, a signal of an enumeration type starts with its leftmost value, e.g., IDLE, so the RTL simulation of a VHDL FSM without reset looks fine as well, while the gate-level simulation shows U.







TipExercise: Find the Missing Reset
