Which flip-flop cells does Yosys use, and how are their reset inputs connected? For the controller with reset, Yosys chooses a one-hot encoding (Section 2.5.9). Does it do so here? In which cycles are busy_o and done_o unknown?
Which of the simulations reveal the bug, and what does each of them show? How do you fix it?



Before continuing, please finish the previous exercise. Once you are done, compare with the solution below.






TipSolution: Find the Missing Reset






state_q is xx in cycle 0 only:
cycle 0: state_q=xx busy_o=0 done_o=0
cycle 1: state_q=00 busy_o=0 done_o=0
cycle 2: state_q=00 busy_o=0 done_o=0
cycle 3: state_q=01 busy_o=1 done_o=0
cycle 4: state_q=01 busy_o=1 done_o=0
cycle 5: state_q=10 busy_o=0 done_o=1
cycle 6: state_q=00 busy_o=0 done_o=0
cycle 7: state_q=00 busy_o=0 done_o=0
The outputs are assigned 0 by default before the case, and no case item matches xx, so they keep their defaults. The default branch moves the FSM to StIdle at the first clock edge. Icarus Verilog prints a “sorry” message that it ignores the unique qualifier (Section 2.5.8), which does not change the result.
With the default start values, Verilator prints the same trace, except that state_q is already 00 in cycle 0. With random start values, the ten seeds of Verilator 5.052 start in all four codes: seeds 1 and 10 in StIdle (00), seeds 2 and 5 in the unused code 11, seeds 3, 4, 6, 7, and 8 in StRun (01), and seed 9 in StDone (10). Another version of Verilator can map the seeds to other start values. From 11, the default branch returns to StIdle after one cycle. Seed 3 starts in StRun, so busy_o is high from cycle 0 to cycle 4, until last_i ends a run that was never started. Seed 9 starts in StDone, so done_o is high in cycle 0. From cycle 5 on, all runs are identical.
With bit [1:0], Icarus Verilog starts state_q at 00, and the trace no longer shows any x, just like Verilator. A two-state type thus hides a missing reset in every simulator, which is why registers should be of type logic.
Yosys maps the design onto 8 cells, among them two sg13cmos5l_dfrbpq_1 flip-flops. Since the RTL has no reset, their RESET_B inputs are tied to 1'h1. Yosys keeps the binary encoding: its FSM detection reports “Not marking ctrl_fsm_noreset.state_q as FSM state register: Circuit seems to be self-resetting”, because the default branch returns every unknown state to StIdle, and it leaves such a register alone. In the gate-level simulation, busy_o is unknown in cycles 0 to 2, and done_o in cycle 0:
cycle 0: busy_o=x done_o=x
cycle 1: busy_o=x done_o=0
cycle 2: busy_o=x done_o=0
cycle 3: busy_o=1 done_o=0
The default branch does not help here, since in the netlist, gates compute the next state, and they propagate the unknown state. After the first clock edge, the state can only be StIdle or StRun (every other state leads to StIdle), so done_o is known to be 0, while busy_o stays x. In cycle 2, start_i moves both possible states to StRun. The gate-level simulation is exact here: an output is x exactly where the chip can show either value. Icarus Verilog also prints 68 “sorry: ifnone with an edge-sensitive path is not supported” messages for the timing blocks of the cell models, which -gno-specify skips anyway, and Yosys reports “ABC: Warning: The network is combinational”. Neither affects the result.
The RTL simulation in Icarus Verilog, Verilator with its default start values, and a two-state type all hide the bug. The gate-level simulation reveals it: it shows which outputs are undefined after power-up. The random start values show the concrete wrong behaviors, a run and a done_o pulse that nobody started. The fix is the reset of the original ctrl_fsm (Section 2.5.9).

title: VLSI Design
section: 3.4 FPGA Habits That Break on an ASIC

title: VLSI Design
text:
3.5 Macro Boundaries
A chip built with the AMS chip template consists of macros that are hardened separately and then assembled into the chip top level (Section 1.10). Two properties of a macro boundary decide how easy this assembly is: whether the timing of a macro depends on its neighbors, and whether the macro can be verified at gate level with its RTL testbench.

3.5.1 Registered Inputs and Outputs
When LibreLane hardens a macro, it does not know the logic outside. It assumes that the environment uses a fixed part of the clock period on each side: the constraints of the template set the input and output delays to IO_DELAY_CONSTRAINT, by default 20 % of the clock period, i.e., 4 ns of the 20 ns period of the counter macro. A path from an input to a register of the macro may then use the remaining 80 %, and a combinational path from an input to an output only 60 %, both a little less after the setup time and the clock uncertainty. If the logic outside is slower than assumed, the chip fails timing, although every macro met its own constraints. Figure 13 (a) shows such a path through two macros.








Figure 13: Two macros, hardened separately. (a) Without registers at the boundary, one timing path (red) runs from a register in macro A through the logic of both macros to a register in macro B. Neither macro sees the whole path, so each one is hardened with an assumed delay for the other part. (b) With registered outputs and inputs, every path through logic stays inside one macro, and the connection between the macros is a plain wire from register to register, which is easy to time at the top level.





With registered outputs, every output of a macro comes directly from a flip-flop, Figure 13 (b). The paths through the logic of a macro end at this register, and the next macro sees a stable signal right after the clock edge, so the timing of each macro depends only on its own logic. What remains between the macros is a wire from register to register, which has almost a full clock cycle and is easy to time at the top level. Outputs from flip-flops are also free of glitches, which matters when they drive a pad, another clock domain, or an asynchronous input. Register the inputs as well when they come from another macro far away on the die, so that the long wire gets a full clock cycle. Asynchronous inputs from pads need a synchronizer anyway (Section 8). The price is a clock cycle of latency for every register stage.


3.5.2 Ports That Survive Synthesis
The template simulates a macro with the same cocotb testbench at RTL and at gate level, the latter with make sim-gl-cocotb (Table 19). This only works if the testbench sees the same interface in both cases:

Plain logic vectors at the top-level ports. Inside the macro, structures, enumerations, and arrays are fine, but after synthesis, every port is a plain vector of bits, and a testbench that relies on a structure or an interface at the top level cannot drive the netlist.
No top-level parameters that the testbench changes. The netlist is synthesized for one set of parameter values, and the gate-level testbench must use exactly these values. A testbench that sets a parameter, such as DIV = 4 in led_blink_tb.py, needs a netlist synthesized with that value.
Access only the ports. Internal names do not reliably survive synthesis and place and route. In the synthesized netlist of the template counter, the outputs of the flip-flops are still called counter_value_o, but in its final netlist, they are net3 to net10 (Section 3.2). A testbench that reads an internal signal works at RTL and fails at gate level.
A reset at the start of every test, and no reliance on initial values, since the netlist starts as x.

title: VLSI Design
VLSI Design
text:
3.7 Checklist for Synthesizable, ASIC-Ready RTL
The coding guidelines of Section 2.9 make your RTL correct and readable. The following checklist adds the guidelines of this chapter, which make it ready for an ASIC:

Every register that holds control state has a reset. Data registers may stay without reset if they are written before they are read.
No initial values and no initial blocks in RTL.
No 'x assignments. Every variable gets a defined default value.
One clock per macro if possible. No clock comes from a register or from logic: a clock enable replaces a divided clock.
Memories with more than a few hundred bits are SRAM macros. Flip-flop arrays are for small memories and for memories with several read ports.
No internal tri-states. Tri-states only exist in the pads.
Every output of a macro comes from a flip-flop. Inputs from far away get a register, asynchronous inputs from pads a synchronizer.
The top-level ports are plain logic vectors, and the testbench accesses only the ports.
The architecture comes first. Compare the candidates with a quick synthesis and timing analysis before you optimize the code.
Simulate with more than one tool: Icarus Verilog with four values, Verilator with random start values, and the netlist at gate level.

title: VLSI Design
text:
3.8 Summary

You verify the RTL, but the chip implements the netlist. Their simulations must agree, and the guidelines of this chapter remove the most common causes of a mismatch.
Simulators approximate the unknown value x: if and a case with a defined default are optimistic and hide an unknown select or state, a default that assigns x is pessimistic, the conditional operator matches the multiplexer cell, and Verilator replaces every x by a two-state value. Never assign 'x in RTL, and do not trust an RTL simulation without x.
A missing reset hides in the RTL simulation. Random start values in Verilator and the gate-level simulation reveal it. Reset all control state. In SG13CMOS5L, every flip-flop has a reset input anyway.
FPGA habits do not carry over: initial values are dropped by synthesis without a warning, a divided clock creates a second clock with its own tree, an inferred memory is built from flip-flops with about ten times the area of an SRAM macro, and an internal tri-state bus either fails to synthesize or risks shorts and floating nodes.
Replace a divided clock by a clock enable: every rising edge of the slow clock becomes a one-cycle pulse that enables registers on the main clock.
Register the outputs of every macro, so that its timing does not depend on its neighbors, and keep the top-level ports plain, so that the same testbench runs on the netlist.
The architecture decides area and speed. For the exclusive counter, the binary version is the smallest, the one-hot ring the fastest, and the Johnson counter lies in between. Two codings of the same architecture gave the same netlist.

In Section 4, we take the testbenches of the last two chapters to a systematic verification methodology, including the gate-level simulation of a netlist with the same testbench.

title: VLSI Design
text:
4.1 Learning Objectives
After this chapter, you will be able to:

distinguish verification, test, and validation, and name what each verification method can prove
write a verification plan that gives each feature of a specification a check and a coverage goal
structure a cocotb testbench into generator, driver, monitor, reference model, scoreboard, and coverage
choose between directed, exhaustive, and constrained-random stimuli, estimate the run time of an exhaustive test, and reproduce a random test from its seed
measure code coverage with Verilator and functional coverage in Python, and explain why full coverage does not prove a correct design
write SystemVerilog assertions in a separate checker, attach them with bind, and know which open-source tools support them
judge the quality of a testbench with mutation testing
run the same testbench on the synthesized netlist, without and with the cell delays of an SDF file, and explain why a timing simulation does not replace static timing analysis
set up a regression that fails when a test fails

title: VLSI Design
text:
4.2 Why Verification Matters
A chip cannot be patched. A bug in software is fixed with an update, but a bug in the masks of an ASIC is in every die of the wafer. The fix takes a new tapeout: new masks, a new run through the fab, new packaging, and new tests, which costs months and, in advanced technologies, millions of euros. The cost of a bug grows with every step of the flow that it passes. At RTL, a fix takes minutes and a new simulation. After synthesis or layout, it takes another run of the flow. On silicon, it takes a new tapeout. This is why verification takes a large share of the effort in every ASIC project, often more than writing the RTL.
Three terms are easily confused:

Verification asks whether the design does what its specification says. It works on models of the chip, i.e., the RTL, the netlist, and the layout, and it happens before the tapeout. This chapter covers functional verification, which checks the logic behavior of the design, cycle by cycle.
Test asks whether a manufactured die is free of defects. It runs on every die after fabrication, with test patterns that the design for test of Section 9 prepares. A test assumes that the design itself is correct.
Validation asks whether the chip does what its application needs, e.g., on a board with real signals and software. It happens with the first silicon.

Verification has several methods, and each one answers a different question (Table 24).



Table 24: Methods of design verification











Method
Question it answers
Limit
In this course




Simulation
Does the design behave correctly for the applied stimuli?

this chapter


Logic equivalence checking
Does the netlist implement the same function as the RTL?

Section 5


Static timing analysis
Does every path meet its timing constraint?

Section 6


Formal property checking
Does a property hold for every possible input sequence?

Simulation remains the workhorse. It works for every design and at every level, from the RTL to the netlist with delays. Its fundamental limit is just as clear: a simulation can show that a bug exists, but never that no bug is left. Everything in this chapter aims at making the simulated stimuli count: checking every output automatically, steering the stimuli into the corners of the design, and measuring what they have reached.

title: VLSI Design
text:
4.4 The Verification Plan
Before writing a testbench, write down what has to be verified. A verification plan lists the features of the specification and gives each one a check, i.e., how the testbench notices a failure, and a coverage goal, i.e., how you know that the stimulus has exercised the feature. The verification is complete when every check passes and every coverage goal is reached, not when the testbench runs without errors. A testbench without checks also runs without errors. Table 25 shows the plan for the FIFO, and the rest of this chapter builds the testbench, the assertions, and the coverage measurement that it asks for.

title: VLSI Design
text:
4.5 Anatomy of a Testbench
The testbenches of Section 2.6 drive the inputs and check the outputs in one loop. That works for a small block, but it mixes three concerns: which operations to apply, how to apply them at the pins, and what the correct answer is. Larger testbenches separate them into the blocks of Figure 16. They work with transactions, i.e., operations at a higher level than single pin values, e.g., “push the value 0x11”:

The generator creates the transactions, as a directed list or at random (Section 4.6).
The driver turns each transaction into pin values at the inputs of the design under test (DUT), at the right time.
The monitor observes the pins at the inputs and outputs of the DUT and turns them back into transactions. It never drives a signal.
The reference model computes what the DUT must do. It is written from the specification, not from the RTL, and it is much simpler than the RTL, because it does not have to be synthesizable.
The scoreboard compares what the DUT did with what the model expects, and reports every difference.
The coverage collector counts which situations the stimulus has reached (Section 4.7).









Figure 16: Architecture of a self-checking testbench. The generator creates transactions, and the driver turns each one into pin values at the inputs of the design under test (DUT). The monitor observes the pins at the inputs and outputs and turns them back into transactions. The reference model computes what the DUT must do, the scoreboard compares it with what the DUT did, and the coverage collector counts which situations the stimulus has reached.





In industry, testbenches with this structure are written in SystemVerilog with the Universal Verification Methodology (UVM) (IEEE 2020), a class library with a standard set of base classes for all these blocks. cocotb builds the same structure from plain Python, and the IIC-OSIC-TOOLS image also contains pyuvm (pyuvm developers 2026), an implementation of UVM in Python on top of cocotb. For the FIFO, a few functions and one class are enough:


fifo/testbenches/cocotb/fifo_tb.py

# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Simon Dorrer
# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
# Description: cocotb testbench for the FIFO with a driver, a monitor,
# a reference model, a scoreboard, and functional coverage.
# Environment variables: SIM=verilator builds with code coverage, and
# SVA=1 adds the assertions of testbenches/sva. GL=1 (Icarus only)
# simulates the netlist fifo.nl.v of the macro folder, SDF=1 adds the
# delays of fifo.sdf. CLK_PERIOD_NS sets the clock (default 20), and
# CHECK=0 switches the scoreboard checks off.

import os
import random
from collections import Counter, deque
from pathlib import Path

import cocotb
from cocotb.clock import Clock
from cocotb.triggers import ClockCycles, FallingEdge, ReadOnly
from cocotb_tools.runner import get_results, get_runner

DEPTH = 4
WIDTH = 8
CLK_PERIOD_NS = float(os.getenv("CLK_PERIOD_NS", "20"))
CHECK = os.getenv("CHECK", "1") == "1"


class Scoreboard:
    """Reference model of the specification, checks, and coverage."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.model = deque()  # oldest entry first
        self.coverage = Counter()

    def check(self, full, empty, data):
        """Compare the outputs of the DUT with the model."""
        n = len(self.model)
        assert full == (n == DEPTH), f"full_o = {full}, {n} entries"
        assert empty == (n == 0), f"empty_o = {empty}, {n} entries"
        if n > 0:
            assert data == self.model[0], \
                f"data_o = {data}, expected {self.model[0]:0{WIDTH}b}"

    def update(self, push, data, pop):
        """Count coverage, then apply one clock edge to the model."""
        full, empty = len(self.model) == DEPTH, len(self.model) == 0
        state = "full" if full else "empty" if empty else "partial"
        op = ["idle", "pop", "push", "push+pop"][2 * push + pop]
        self.coverage[f"{op} when {state}"] += 1
        if pop and not empty:
            self.model.popleft()
        if push and not full:  # a full FIFO refuses a push
            self.model.append(data)


async def monitor(dut, sb):
    """Sample the DUT at every falling edge, after the driver."""
    while True:
        await ReadOnly()
        if CHECK:
            sb.check(dut.full_o.value, dut.empty_o.value,
                     dut.data_o.value)
        sb.update(int(dut.push_i.value), int(dut.data_i.value),
                  int(dut.pop_i.value))
        await FallingEdge(dut.clk_i)


async def driver(dut, transactions):
    """Apply one (push, data, pop) transaction per clock cycle."""
    for push, data, pop in transactions:
        dut.push_i.value = push
        dut.data_i.value = data
        dut.pop_i.value = pop
        await FallingEdge(dut.clk_i)
    dut.push_i.value = 0
    dut.pop_i.value = 0
    await ClockCycles(dut.clk_i, 2)


async def start_up(dut):
    """Start the clock, reset the DUT, and start the monitor."""
    cocotb.start_soon(Clock(dut.clk_i, CLK_PERIOD_NS, "ns").start())
    dut.rst_ni.value = 0
    dut.push_i.value = 0
    dut.data_i.value = 0
    dut.pop_i.value = 0
    await ClockCycles(dut.clk_i, 2)
    await FallingEdge(dut.clk_i)
    dut.rst_ni.value = 1
    sb = Scoreboard()
    cocotb.start_soon(monitor(dut, sb))
    return sb


def report(sb):
    """Log the coverage bins, return the bins that were never hit."""
    bins = [f"{op} when {state}"
            for op in ("idle", "push", "pop", "push+pop")
            for state in ("empty", "partial", "full")]
    for name in bins:
        cocotb.log.info(f"{name:24s} {sb.coverage[name]:5d}")
    return [name for name in bins if sb.coverage[name] == 0]


@cocotb.test()
async def test_fill_and_drain(dut):
    """Directed: push DEPTH values, then pop all of them."""
    sb = await start_up(dut)
    values = [0x11 * (i + 1) for i in range(DEPTH)]
    await driver(dut, [(1, v, 0) for v in values]
                 + [(0, 0, 1)] * DEPTH)
    report(sb)


@cocotb.test()
async def test_random(dut):
    """Random: phases of 50 cycles that tend to fill or to drain."""
    sb = await start_up(dut)
    transactions = []
    for _ in range(20):
        p_push = random.choice([0.2, 0.5, 0.8])
        for _ in range(50):
            push = int(random.random() < p_push)
            pop = int(random.random() < 1 - p_push)
            data = random.getrandbits(WIDTH)
            transactions.append((push, data, pop))
    await driver(dut, transactions)
    holes = report(sb)
    assert not holes, f"coverage holes: {holes}"


def fifo_runner():
    sim = os.getenv("SIM", "icarus")
    proj_path = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
    macro_path = proj_path / "../.."

    top = "fifo"
    sources = [macro_path / "rtl/fifo.sv"]
    sva = macro_path / "testbenches/sva/fifo_sva.sv"
    build_args, plusargs = [], []
    if sim == "verilator":
        build_args = ["--coverage"]
        if os.getenv("SVA", "0") == "1":
            sources.append(sva)
    if os.getenv("GL", "0") == "1":
        cells = Path(os.environ["PDK_ROOT"]) \
            / "ihp-sg13cmos5l/libs.ref/sg13cmos5l_stdcell/verilog"
        sources = [cells / "sg13cmos5l_udp.v",
                   cells / "sg13cmos5l_stdcell.v",
                   macro_path / "fifo.nl.v"]
        build_args = ["-gno-specify"]
        if os.getenv("SDF", "0") == "1":
            top = "fifo_sdf"
            sources.append(proj_path / "fifo_sdf.sv")
            build_args = ["-gspecify"]
            sdf_file = (macro_path / "fifo.sdf").resolve()
            plusargs = [f"+SDF={sdf_file}"]

    runner = get_runner(sim)
    runner.build(
        sources=sources,
        hdl_toplevel=top,
        build_args=build_args,
        always=True,
        waves=True,
        timescale=("1ns", "1ps"),
    )
    results_xml = runner.test(
        hdl_toplevel=top,
        test_module="fifo_tb",
        plusargs=plusargs,
        waves=True,
    )

    # A failing test leaves the exit status at 0, so check the results
    num_tests, num_failed = get_results(results_xml)
    if num_failed:
        raise SystemExit(
            f"FAIL: {num_failed} of {num_tests} tests failed")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    fifo_runner()



In this small testbench, the class Scoreboard holds three blocks of Figure 16: the reference model (model and update()), the scoreboard itself (check()), and the coverage collector (coverage, printed by report()). The generator is the list of transactions in each test.
The reference model is a Python deque with the oldest entry first. Compare it with the RTL: no pointers, no wrap bit, and no storage array. This independence is the point. A model that copied the structure of the RTL would also copy its bugs.
check() compares both flags in every cycle and data_o whenever the model holds an entry. It does not check data_o while the FIFO is empty, because the specification leaves it undefined. update() first counts the coverage and then applies one clock edge to the model, with the flags from before the edge, exactly as the specification says.
driver() applies one transaction per clock cycle, right after the falling edge, as in Section 2.6.
monitor() runs in parallel with the test, started with cocotb.start_soon(). At every falling edge, it waits for ReadOnly(), the phase at the end of a time step in which all signals have settled and no process may write anymore. At that moment, the outputs show the state after the last rising edge, and the inputs show what the driver has just applied for the next one. So the monitor first checks the outputs against the model, and then updates the model with the inputs. Without ReadOnly(), the monitor would still see the inputs from before the writes of the driver, because cocotb applies writes later in the time step.
A failing assert in the monitor fails the test that is running, with the message of the assertion.
test_fill_and_drain is a directed test and test_random a random one (Section 4.6). Both print the coverage at the end.
The runner reads the environment variables listed at the top of the file. They select the simulator, the assertions, and the netlist with or without delays, which the following sections use.

Run the testbench in its folder:
cd /foss/designs/vlsi-design/content/verification/code/fifo
cd testbenches/cocotb
COCOTB_RANDOM_SEED=1 python3 fifo_tb.py
cd ../..
Both tests pass, and each one prints a table of its coverage bins, which Section 4.7 explains. COCOTB_RANDOM_SEED fixes the random numbers (Section 4.6.3).

title: VLSI Design
text:
4.6 Stimulus
A testbench is only as good as its stimulus: a bug that the stimulus never activates cannot be found by any check. There are three basic kinds of stimuli, and good testbenches combine them.

4.6.1 Directed Tests
A directed test applies a sequence that a person has written for one feature. test_fill_and_drain pushes four values and pops them again. Directed tests are easy to read and to debug, and they are the right tool for a known corner case, e.g., the reset or the largest value of a counter. Their weakness: they test exactly what their author thought of, and the author of a testbench tends to think of the same cases as the author of the RTL, who is often the same person.


4.6.2 Exhaustive Tests
The ideal stimulus applies every possible input. For a combinational block with \(n\) input bits, these are \(2^n\) input vectors, and an exhaustive test proves the function, at least in simulation. The number grows quickly. A 16-bit multiplier has \(2^{32} \approx 4.3 \cdot 10^{9}\) combinations of its two operands, and a 32-bit adder \(2^{64} \approx 1.8 \cdot 10^{19}\). At 100,000 vectors per second, a good rate for a cocotb testbench, the exhaustive test of the multiplier takes about half a day, and that of the adder almost six million years.
For sequential circuits, it is worse, because the outputs depend on the sequence of all previous inputs. The FIFO has 10 input bits (push_i, pop_i, and data_i), so there are \(2^{10} = 1024\) possible inputs in every cycle and \(1024^{10} \approx 1.3 \cdot 10^{30}\) different sequences of only ten cycles. Exhaustive simulation is therefore limited to small combinational blocks, and to small parameter values of a parameterized design.


4.6.3 Random Tests
A random test applies a large number of random inputs. It finds bugs in cases that nobody thought of, at a low cost per test. The random numbers come from a pseudo-random number generator, whose sequence is fully determined by its start value, the seed. cocotb seeds the random module of Python at the start of every run, from the time or from the environment variable COCOTB_RANDOM_SEED, and prints the seed at the start of the simulation, e.g., Seeding Python random module with 1793394914. When a random test fails, rerun it with this seed to reproduce the failure exactly:
COCOTB_RANDOM_SEED=1793394914 python3 fifo_tb.py
This works only as long as the testbench draws its random numbers in the same order, so fix the bug before you change the testbench. All results of this chapter use seed 1.
Purely random inputs are not always good stimuli. The interesting states of a design are often reached only by a particular sequence, e.g., a deep FIFO is full only after many more pushes than pops. test_random therefore uses constrained-random stimuli. It runs 20 phases of 50 cycles, i.e., 1000 cycles, and each phase draws the probability of a push from 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8 and sets the probability of a pop to the complement. A phase with mostly pushes fills the FIFO, and a phase with mostly pops drains it. The constraints steer the stimuli toward the corners, and the random values within them still reach combinations that nobody has written down. SystemVerilog has a whole constraint language for this (rand, constraint, and randomize()), and in Python, plain code does the job.
The best tests combine directed and random values: directed values at the corners of every input, i.e., the smallest and the largest value, single bits, and the boundaries of every range, followed by random values. The following exercise shows why.






TipExercise: Verify a Barrel Shifter



The folder barrel_shift contains a combinational barrel shifter in rtl/barrel_shift.sv. It has the parameter WIDTH (a power of two, default 8), the inputs data_i (WIDTH bits), shamt_i ($clog2(WIDTH) bits), and mode_i (2 bits), and the output data_o. mode_i selects a shift left (00), a shift right (01), a rotation left (10), or a rotation right (11) of data_i by shamt_i positions, and a shift fills the free positions with zeros. The folder testbenches/cocotb holds the reference solution, so move it out of the way first. All commands start in the folder barrel_shift:
cd /foss/designs/vlsi-design/content/verification/code/barrel_shift
mv testbenches/cocotb/barrel_shift_tb.py barrel_shift_tb_solution.py

Draw the testbench for the barrel shifter in the style of Figure 16. Which blocks does a combinational DUT need, and which ones merge?
Write a cocotb testbench testbenches/cocotb/barrel_shift_tb.py with a reference model in Python and a test test_exhaustive, which applies all input vectors of the 8-bit version. Let the runner read WIDTH from an environment variable (default 8) and pass it to the DUT as a parameter, and skip the exhaustive test for WIDTH above 8 with the decorator @cocotb.test(skip=WIDTH > 8). Run the testbench with Icarus Verilog and with Verilator, and note the run time of the test, which cocotb prints in its summary.
Estimate from your measurement how long the exhaustive test would take for WIDTH = 16 and for WIDTH = 32.
Add a test test_random. It first applies corner values (zero, all ones, only the lowest bit, only the highest bit, and alternating bits, each with the shift amounts 0, 1, and WIDTH - 1 and all four modes) and then 10,000 random vectors. Run it with WIDTH=32.
The file exercise/barrel_shift_bug.sv contains the module barrel_shift_bug, with the same ports and one bug. Let your runner select it with the environment variable TOPLEVEL=barrel_shift_bug, as the testbenches of Section 3 do, and run both tests with WIDTH 8 and 32. Which test finds the bug, and why does the other one miss it? Then lint the file, once without and once with -GWIDTH=32.

The commands of steps 2, 4, and 5:
cd testbenches/cocotb
python3 barrel_shift_tb.py                 # Icarus Verilog
SIM=verilator python3 barrel_shift_tb.py   # Verilator
WIDTH=32 python3 barrel_shift_tb.py
TOPLEVEL=barrel_shift_bug python3 barrel_shift_tb.py
TOPLEVEL=barrel_shift_bug WIDTH=32 python3 barrel_shift_tb.py
cd ../..
verilator --lint-only -Wall exercise/barrel_shift_bug.sv
verilator --lint-only -Wall -GWIDTH=32 exercise/barrel_shift_bug.sv


Before continuing, please finish the previous exercise. Once you are done, compare with the solution below.






TipSolution: Verify a Barrel Shifter






The generator creates the input vectors, in nested loops or at random. Since the DUT has no clock and no state, the driver and the monitor merge into one function: apply a vector, wait for the logic to settle, and read the output. The reference model computes the expected output from the same vector, and an assert compares them as the scoreboard. In the listing below, check() does all of this in one short function.
The reference testbench:



barrel_shift/testbenches/cocotb/barrel_shift_tb.py

# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Simon Dorrer
# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
# Description: Self-checking cocotb testbench for barrel_shift with a
# Python reference model, an exhaustive test (WIDTH <= 8 only), and a
# random test with corner values. WIDTH (default 8) sets the DUT
# parameter, TOPLEVEL=barrel_shift_bug selects the exercise version.

import os
import random
import time
from pathlib import Path

import cocotb
from cocotb.triggers import Timer
from cocotb_tools.runner import get_results, get_runner

WIDTH = int(os.getenv("WIDTH", "8"))
MASK = (1 << WIDTH) - 1
NUM_RANDOM = 10_000


def model(data, shamt, mode):
    """Reference model: what barrel_shift must compute."""
    if mode == 0:
        return (data << shamt) & MASK
    if mode == 1:
        return data >> shamt
    if mode == 2:
        return ((data << shamt) | (data >> (WIDTH - shamt))) & MASK
    return ((data >> shamt) | (data << (WIDTH - shamt))) & MASK


async def check(dut, data, shamt, mode):
    """Apply one input vector and compare data_o with the model."""
    dut.data_i.value = data
    dut.shamt_i.value = shamt
    dut.mode_i.value = mode
    await Timer(1, "ns")
    expected = model(data, shamt, mode)
    assert dut.data_o.value == expected, (
        f"data {data:#x}, shamt {shamt}, mode {mode}: "
        f"expected {expected:0{WIDTH}b}, got {dut.data_o.value}")


@cocotb.test(skip=WIDTH > 8)
async def test_exhaustive(dut):
    """All 2**WIDTH * WIDTH * 4 input vectors."""
    start = time.perf_counter()
    for data in range(1 << WIDTH):
        for shamt in range(WIDTH):
            for mode in range(4):
                await check(dut, data, shamt, mode)
    num = (1 << WIDTH) * WIDTH * 4
    rate = num / (time.perf_counter() - start)
    cocotb.log.info(f"{num} vectors, {rate:.0f} vectors/s")


@cocotb.test()
async def test_random(dut):
    """Corner values first, then NUM_RANDOM random vectors."""
    corners = [0, MASK, 1, 1 << (WIDTH - 1), 0x5555_5555 & MASK]
    for data in corners:
        for shamt in (0, 1, WIDTH - 1):
            for mode in range(4):
                await check(dut, data, shamt, mode)
    for _ in range(NUM_RANDOM):
        await check(dut, random.getrandbits(WIDTH),
                    random.randrange(WIDTH), random.randrange(4))


def barrel_shift_runner():
    sim = os.getenv("SIM", "icarus")
    top = os.getenv("TOPLEVEL", "barrel_shift")
    proj_path = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
    folder = "exercise" if top == "barrel_shift_bug" else "rtl"

    runner = get_runner(sim)
    runner.build(
        sources=[proj_path / f"../../{folder}/{top}.sv"],
        hdl_toplevel=top,
        parameters={"WIDTH": WIDTH},
        always=True,
        timescale=("1ns", "1ps"),
    )
    results_xml = runner.test(
        hdl_toplevel=top,
        test_module="barrel_shift_tb",
    )

    # A failing test leaves the exit status at 0, so check the results
    num_tests, num_failed = get_results(results_xml)
    if num_failed:
        raise SystemExit(
            f"FAIL: {num_failed} of {num_tests} tests failed")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    barrel_shift_runner()


The model uses the unlimited integers of Python and masks the result to WIDTH bits. For a rotation by 0, it shifts by WIDTH in the other direction, which gives 0, as in the RTL. check() applies a vector, waits 1 ns, and compares. The exhaustive test of the 8-bit version applies \(2^8 \cdot 8 \cdot 4 = 8192\) vectors in about 0.1 s, i.e., about 70,000 vectors per second with Icarus Verilog and 100,000 with Verilator. For such a small DUT, the Python side of cocotb limits the rate, so Verilator is only about 1.4 times faster.

The 16-bit version has \(2^{16} \cdot 16 \cdot 4\) = 4,194,304 vectors, which takes about one minute (measured with the skip limit raised to 16: 64 s with Icarus Verilog and 47 s with Verilator). The 32-bit version has \(2^{32} \cdot 32 \cdot 4 \approx 5.5 \cdot 10^{11}\) vectors, which would take two to three months at these rates.
test_random passes for WIDTH=32.
With WIDTH 8, both tests pass. With WIDTH 32, test_random fails at the first corner vector with the shift amount 31 and nonzero data: data 0xffffffff, shamt 31, mode 0 gives 11111111111111111111111110000000 instead of a 1 followed by 31 zeros. The data was shifted by 7 instead of 31 positions. The bug is the declaration logic [2:0] sh: three bits are enough for WIDTH = 8, but for WIDTH = 32 the assignment cuts shamt_i down to its three lower bits. The exhaustive test is a complete proof for the 8-bit instance, but it says nothing about the 32-bit one. Verilator lint is clean with the default parameter, and it reports WIDTHTRUNC (and UNUSEDSIGNAL for shamt_i[4:3]) only with -GWIDTH=32. Verilator even refuses to build the 32-bit version for cocotb: SIM=verilator stops at the warning WIDTHTRUNC, which it treats as an error, before any test runs. Lint and simulate every parameter value that you use. An exhaustive test at a small parameter value complements a random test at the real one, but does not replace it.

title: VLSI Design
text:
4.7 Coverage
Coverage answers the question of when the verification is complete. It measures what the stimuli have reached. Two kinds complement each other: code coverage, which the simulator measures on the RTL, and functional coverage, which the testbench measures on the specification.

4.7.1 Code Coverage
Code coverage needs no work in the testbench. The simulator counts how often each part of the RTL was exercised. Verilator distinguishes:

line coverage: was every block of statements executed?
branch coverage: did every if, case, and conditional operator take each of its branches?
expression coverage: did the terms of every logical expression, e.g., push_i and full_o in push_i && !full_o, take the values that decide its result?
toggle coverage: did every bit of every signal change from 0 to 1 and from 1 to 0?

The runner of fifo_tb.py builds with --coverage when you select Verilator, and the simulation writes the counts into sim_build/coverage.dat. The tool verilator_coverage summarizes them and writes a copy of the RTL with the counts in front of every line. The environment variable COCOTB_TEST_FILTER selects the tests to run by name, here only the directed one:
cd /foss/designs/vlsi-design/content/verification/code/fifo
cd testbenches/cocotb
SIM=verilator COCOTB_TEST_FILTER=test_fill_and_drain \
  python3 fifo_tb.py
verilator_coverage --annotate-min 1 --annotate-points \
  --annotate annotated sim_build/coverage.dat
Coverage Summary:                (excerpt)
  line      : 100.0% (  3/  3)
  toggle    : 50.7% ( 69/136)
  branch    : 100.0% (  8/  8)
  expr      : 100.0% ( 14/ 14)
The directed test reaches 100 % line, branch, and expression coverage. The full expression coverage is surprising, since the test never pushes into a full FIFO. But Verilator counts a term as covered when it alone decides the result: the point (full_o==1) => 0 of push_i && !full_o is hit whenever the FIFO is full, with or without a push. Only the toggle coverage shows a gap. The annotated copy annotated/fifo.sv marks every partially covered line by ~ and, thanks to --annotate-points, lists the points below it, e.g.:
~000002   logic [AW:0]      wr_ptr_d, wr_ptr_q, rd_ptr_d, rd_ptr_q;
-000000  point: type=toggle comment=wr_ptr_q[2]:1->0 hier=fifo
The wrap bits of both pointers rise once but never fall, because four pushes and four pops wrap each pointer only once. Bits 3 and 7 of data_i and data_o never toggle, because none of the four values 0x11 to 0x44 sets them, and the storage bits only rise, because each entry is written once. With both tests, the toggle coverage also reaches 100 % (136 of 136 points).


4.7.2 Functional Coverage
Code coverage measures the RTL. It cannot see a situation that the specification names but the RTL handles without a line of its own, and it cannot see a feature that the RTL lacks altogether. Functional coverage measures the situations of the specification instead. The verification engineer defines them as cover points and often crosses them, i.e., counts every combination. The FIFO testbench crosses the operation (idle, push, pop, or both) with the fill state (empty, partially filled, or full), which gives the 12 bins of Table 26. Scoreboard.update() counts them, and report() prints them at the end of each test.

The directed test hits only 5 of the 12 bins, although its code coverage looks nearly perfect. It never pushes into a full FIFO, never pops from an empty one, and never pushes and pops in the same cycle. These are exactly the rules of the specification that are easy to get wrong. The random test hits all 12 bins, and it checks this itself: its last line fails the test if a bin was never hit. Such an automatic check of the coverage goals turns the verification plan into code.
Both kinds of coverage have the same limit: they measure what the stimuli have reached, not what the checks have verified. A testbench that drives random inputs and checks nothing reaches the same coverage as one that checks every output. Section 4.9 measures the checks.

title: VLSI Design
text:
4.8 Assertions
An assertion states a property that must always hold, and the simulator checks it all the time. SystemVerilog has two kinds:

An immediate assertion checks a condition at one moment, like an if with an error message, e.g., assert (!(full_o && empty_o)) else $error("full and empty");. It is a statement inside an always or initial block.
A concurrent assertion describes a behavior over time and is checked at every clock edge. SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) are a language of their own for such properties, with sequences of conditions, implications, and functions of past values.

A concurrent assertion has this form:
a_name: assert property (@(posedge clk_i) disable iff (!rst_ni)
  antecedent |=> consequent);

@(posedge clk_i) samples all signals at the rising clock edge, with their values from just before the edge, as a flip-flop does.
disable iff (!rst_ni) switches the assertion off during the reset.
a |-> b (overlapping implication) requires b in the same cycle in which a holds, and a |=> b (non-overlapping implication) in the next cycle. If a does not hold, the property holds.
$stable(x) is true if the sampled value of x equals the one at the previous clock edge, $past(x) returns the sampled value at the previous edge, and $rose(x) and $fell(x) detect a change of the sampled value. Glitches between two clock edges are never seen.
cover property (...) counts how often a property was reached, which is functional coverage written in SVA.

The checker for the FIFO:


fifo/testbenches/sva/fifo_sva.sv

// SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Simon Dorrer
// SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
// Description: Assertions for the FIFO. The bind statement at the end
// adds this checker to every instance of fifo without changing its
// RTL, and the checker can also read the internal pointers.

`default_nettype none

module fifo_sva #(
  parameter int unsigned WIDTH = 8,
  parameter int unsigned DEPTH = 4
) (
  input logic                   clk_i,
  input logic                   rst_ni,
  input logic                   push_i,
  input logic                   pop_i,
  input logic [WIDTH-1:0]       data_o,
  input logic                   full_o,
  input logic                   empty_o,
  input logic [$clog2(DEPTH):0] wr_ptr_q,
  input logic [$clog2(DEPTH):0] rd_ptr_q
);

  logic [$clog2(DEPTH):0] level;
  assign level = wr_ptr_q - rd_ptr_q;

  // Never full and empty at the same time
  a_flags: assert property (@(posedge clk_i) disable iff (!rst_ni)
    !(full_o && empty_o));

  // The fill level never exceeds DEPTH (white box: the pointers)
  a_level: assert property (@(posedge clk_i) disable iff (!rst_ni)
    32'(level) <= DEPTH);

  // The oldest entry does not change without a pop
  a_head: assert property (@(posedge clk_i) disable iff (!rst_ni)
    !empty_o && !pop_i |=> $stable(data_o));

  // A full FIFO refuses a push, so a pop always makes room
  a_room: assert property (@(posedge clk_i) disable iff (!rst_ni)
    full_o && pop_i |=> !full_o);

  // Was a push and a pop on a full FIFO ever tried?
  c_full_push_pop: cover property (@(posedge clk_i)
    disable iff (!rst_ni) full_o && push_i && pop_i);

endmodule

bind fifo fifo_sva #(.WIDTH(WIDTH), .DEPTH(DEPTH)) u_sva (.*);

`default_nettype wire



a_flags: the FIFO is never full and empty at the same time.
a_level: the fill level never exceeds DEPTH. The checker computes it from the internal pointers, so this is a white-box property, which needs a look inside the design. A pop from an empty FIFO makes level wrap around to 7, so a_level also catches it.
a_head: while the FIFO holds an entry and no pop happens, data_o keeps its value in the next cycle. A push writes behind the oldest entry, never on it.
a_room: because a full FIFO refuses a push, a pop on a full FIFO must leave it not full.
c_full_push_pop counts the cycles with a push and a pop on a full FIFO.
The bind statement at the end inserts an instance of fifo_sva into every instance of fifo, as if it were written inside the module. The ports of the checker connect by name (.*) to the signals of fifo with the same names, including the internal pointers. The RTL stays untouched.

Assertions can live in three places. In the RTL, the designer documents an assumption right where it matters, but every tool that reads the RTL has to handle them, including synthesis. In a separate checker attached with bind, as here, the RTL stays clean, and the checker can still read internal signals. In the testbench, as the checks of the cocotb scoreboard, they see only the ports. That is a limitation at RTL and an advantage at gate level: synthesis renames or removes the internal signals and does not translate assertions, so only checks at the ports still work on a netlist. A classic VHDL technique keeps the assertions in a separate entity that observes only the ports, so that its checks also run on the netlist.
The open-source tools support assertions very differently (Table 27).



Table 27: Support of SystemVerilog assertions in the open-source tools










Tool
Immediate assertions
Concurrent assertions




Icarus Verilog 14.0
supported, but $error only prints a message, and the simulation continues and exits with status 0
rejected as not supported (sorry), dropped without a message with -gsupported-assertions, and the non-overlapping implication and bind are syntax errors


Verilator 5.052
supported
supported, at least the properties of this chapter, and checked by default (--no-assert switches them off). A failure stops the simulation.


Yosys 0.70 (read_verilog -sv)
syntax error at else
syntax error at @(posedge ...)


Yosys 0.70 with slang
read without an error
unsupported SVA feature for the non-overlapping implication






Hence the rules of this course: keep concurrent assertions out of rtl/, in a checker file that only Verilator reads, and keep the checks at the ports in the cocotb testbench, which runs with every simulator and on the netlist. The runner adds the checker with SVA=1:
SIM=verilator SVA=1 COCOTB_RANDOM_SEED=1 python3 fifo_tb.py
verilator_coverage --annotate annotated sim_build/coverage.dat
Both tests pass, and sim_build/coverage.dat now also holds the count of the cover property, which the annotated copy annotated/fifo_sva.sv shows in front of its line. With seed 1, c_full_push_pop counts 54, the same number as the bin push+pop when full of the Python coverage. When an assertion fails, Verilator prints a line such as %Error: fifo_sva.sv:40: Assertion failed in fifo.u_sva.a_room and stops the simulation. cocotb then reports SimFailure: ... the simulation ended prematurely for the running test and for every test after it, which never run, and the runner ends with a Python traceback instead of its FAIL line.
Do assertions find more bugs than the scoreboard? Not in this testbench. Our scoreboard checks every output in every cycle, so a bug that reaches an output is reported at the next falling edge, half a cycle before an assertion can fire at the next rising edge. Assertions pay off where a scoreboard is blind or absent: they check internal state such as the pointers, they name the rule that was broken instead of a wrong output value, and they keep working when the FIFO sits deep inside a larger design without a FIFO scoreboard, because bind attaches the checker to every instance. Formal property checking tools, such as SymbiYosys, which is also in the image, can even prove an assertion for every input sequence. This course uses formal methods only for equivalence checking (Section 5).

title: VLSI Design
text:
4.9 Mutation Testing
Coverage measures the stimuli, but what measures the checks? Mutation testing inserts a small deliberate bug into the design, a mutant, and reruns the testbench. If a test fails, the mutant is killed. If all tests pass, the mutant survives, and there are only two possible reasons: the testbench has a hole, or the mutant does not change the behavior at the ports at all, in which case it is called equivalent. The share of killed mutants among the non-equivalent ones measures the quality of the testbench.
An example: replace if (push) by if (push_i) in the storage process of fifo.sv. The storage is now also written by a push into a full FIFO, where the write pointer addresses the oldest entry, so the push overwrites it. Whether a test notices depends on its stimulus, which the following exercise measures.
Mutants are usually created by tools. The IIC-OSIC-TOOLS image contains MCY (Mutation Cover with Yosys) (YosysHQ 2026b), which creates mutants of a design with Yosys and runs a testbench on each of them. For a small design, a handful of mutants written by hand already shows the holes of a testbench, as the following exercise shows.






TipExercise: Kill the Mutants



Each of the following six mutants changes one statement of rtl/fifo.sv, M6 the two reset assignments. All commands start in the folder content/verification/code/fifo.

M1: push = push_i && !full_o; becomes push = push_i;
M2: pop = pop_i && !empty_o; becomes pop = pop_i;
M3: push = push_i && !full_o; becomes push = push_i && (!full_o || pop_i);
M4: if (push) begin becomes if (push_i) begin
M5: (wr_ptr_q == rd_ptr_q) becomes (wr_ptr_q[1:0] == rd_ptr_q[1:0])
M6: in the reset branch, '0 becomes '1 for both pointers


For each mutant, edit rtl/fifo.sv and run the first command below in the folder testbenches/cocotb. Which tests kill the mutant? Restore the original afterwards with git restore rtl/fifo.sv in the folder fifo.
Also run each mutant with the assertions alone, i.e., without the checks of the scoreboard (second command). Which assertion fires first? Then run the third command, with Icarus Verilog and without checks. What do you observe?
Explain with Table 26 why test_fill_and_drain misses M1 to M4.
Sketch the fill level of the FIFO over the cycles of test_fill_and_drain, and mark where a push into a full FIFO, a pop from an empty FIFO, and a push with a pop on a full FIFO would fit. Then add at most three transactions to the list in test_fill_and_drain, such that it kills M1 to M5 and still passes with the original design.
Can any test kill M6? Is M6 a wrong design?

COCOTB_RANDOM_SEED=1 python3 fifo_tb.py
SIM=verilator SVA=1 CHECK=0 COCOTB_RANDOM_SEED=1 python3 fifo_tb.py
CHECK=0 COCOTB_RANDOM_SEED=1 python3 fifo_tb.py


Before continuing, please finish the previous exercise. Once you are done, compare with the solution below.

The first message of the scoreboard is full_o = 1, 3 entries for M1 and M3, empty_o = 0, 0 entries for M2, data_o = 10111011, expected 11011000 for M4, and empty_o = 1, 4 entries for M5. The scoreboard kills M1 to M5, and so do the assertions alone. For M4, the scoreboard reports the wrong data_o at 2370 ns (2150 ns after the start of test_random, which begins at 220 ns), half a cycle before a_head at 2380 ns. With CHECK=0 and Icarus Verilog, every mutant passes both tests: without checks, a testbench verifies nothing, whatever its coverage.

The four mutants M1 to M4 need a push or a pop at a boundary of the fill level: M1 and M4 a push into a full FIFO, M2 a pop from an empty FIFO, and M3 a push and a pop on a full FIFO. The bins push when full, pop when empty, and push+pop when full of the directed test are all 0. The coverage holes predicted the surviving mutants. M6 survives for another reason (step 5).
After the four pushes, a push into the full FIFO kills M1 and M4, and a push with a pop on the full FIFO removes 0x11, refuses 0x66, and kills M3. The four pops then remove 0x22, 0x33, and 0x44, and the last one pops the empty FIFO, which kills M2. A final push with a pop on the empty FIFO adds the bin push+pop when empty:

    await driver(dut, [(1, v, 0) for v in values]
                 + [(1, 0x55, 0), (1, 0x66, 1)]
                 + [(0, 0, 1)] * DEPTH
                 + [(1, 0x77, 1)])
The extended test kills M1 to M5 and passes with the original design.

No. M6 starts both pointers at 3'b111 instead of 3'b000. They are still equal after the reset, so the FIFO is empty, and from then on both pointers differ from the original ones by the same constant. Every port behaves as before wherever the specification defines it, so no testbench that checks the specification can tell the difference. Only data_o of an empty FIFO, which the specification leaves undefined, may show another stale entry. M6 is an equivalent mutant, and it is a correct design. A surviving mutant is a hint, not a verdict, and every survivor needs a look: a hole in the testbench, or a change that does not matter.

title: VLSI Design
text:
4.10 Gate-Level Simulation
Section 3.2 explained why the netlist must pass the same testbench as the RTL: the chip implements the netlist. A logic equivalence check (Section 5) proves that the netlist computes the same functions as the RTL, but it cannot see what Section 3 showed in simulation, i.e., unknown start values, a missing reset, and the propagation of x. A gate-level simulation also exercises what only exists in the netlist, e.g., the scan chains of Section 9, and with the cell delays, it gives a second, independent look at the timing. Figure 17 shows its ingredients.








Figure 17: Ingredients of a gate-level simulation. Logic synthesis maps the RTL onto the cells of the Liberty library and writes the netlist. Static timing analysis computes the delay of every cell instance from the tables in the Liberty file and writes it into an SDF file. The simulator combines the netlist, the Verilog models of the cells from the PDK, the delays from the SDF file, and the same testbench as for the RTL. Without the SDF file, every cell switches without delay. After the layout, the SDF file also holds the wire delays.






4.10.1 Without Delays
With GL=1, the runner of fifo_tb.py replaces rtl/fifo.sv by the Verilog models of the standard cells and the netlist fifo.nl.v in the folder fifo, and it works with Icarus Verilog only. It compiles with -gno-specify, which ignores the timing in the cell models, so every cell switches without delay. Synthesize the FIFO with the commands of Section 3 and run the same testbench:
cd /foss/designs/vlsi-design/content/verification/code/fifo
yosys -p "read_verilog -sv rtl/fifo.sv; synth -top fifo; \
  dfflibmap -liberty $LIB; abc -liberty $LIB; opt_clean; \
  stat -liberty $LIB; write_verilog -noattr fifo.nl.v"
cd testbenches/cocotb
GL=1 python3 fifo_tb.py
cd ../..
The netlist has 103 cells with an area of 3008 µm². Among them are 38 flip-flops of the type dfrbpq_1: 6 for the pointers and 32 for the storage, whose reset inputs are tied to 1 (Section 3.3.1). As in Section 3.4.3, the storage also needs 32 2:1 multiplexers that hold the values, and the read port 8 4:1 multiplexers. Both tests pass. As in Section 3.3.1, Icarus Verilog prints 68 sorry messages about the timing of the cell models, which do not matter without delays.
In the waveform sim_build/fifo.fst, data_o is xxxxxxxx after the reset until the first push, at gate level as at RTL, because the storage has no reset. The testbench does not fail, because the specification leaves data_o undefined while the FIFO is empty, and the scoreboard follows the specification. A testbench that compared data_o in every cycle would fail here, on a correct design.


4.10.2 With Delays from an SDF File
For a timing simulation, the cell models need the delay of every cell instance. It depends on the load and on the input slew of each instance, which only a timing analysis knows. Static timing analysis therefore writes the delays into a file in the Standard Delay Format (SDF) (IEEE 2001), and the simulator annotates them to the cell instances, a step called back-annotation. Before the layout, the SDF file holds only the delays of the cells. After the layout, it also holds the delays of the wires, computed from the extracted parasitics (Section 10).
The script syn/sta.tcl runs OpenSTA on the netlist and writes fifo.sdf. Its constraints describe the testbench: a clock period of 20 ns, and inputs and outputs that may use half a period each, because the testbench changes the inputs and samples the outputs at the falling edge. Section 6 explains these commands. For each timing path, the report of OpenSTA lists the time at which the data arrives and the time at which it is required. Their difference is the slack, and a negative slack is a timing violation. The path with the smallest slack is the critical path. Here is the entry of one flip-flop in the SDF file:
 (CELL
  (CELLTYPE "sg13cmos5l_dfrbpq_1")
  (INSTANCE _120_)
  (DELAY
   (ABSOLUTE
    (IOPATH CLK Q (0.159:0.161:0.163) (0.155:0.156:0.158))
    (IOPATH RESET_B Q () (0.000:0.000:0.000))
   )
  )
  (TIMINGCHECK
    (REMOVAL (posedge RESET_B) (posedge CLK) (-0.097:-0.097:-0.097))
    (RECOVERY (posedge RESET_B) (posedge CLK) (0.117:0.117:0.117))
    (SETUP (posedge D) (posedge CLK) (0.117:0.119:0.121))
    (SETUP (negedge D) (posedge CLK) (0.120:0.122:0.124))
    (HOLD (posedge D) (posedge CLK) (-0.062:-0.064:-0.065))
    (HOLD (negedge D) (posedge CLK) (-0.040:-0.042:-0.044))
    (WIDTH (posedge CLK) (0.217:0.217:0.217))
    (WIDTH (negedge CLK) (0.249:0.249:0.249))
    (WIDTH (negedge RESET_B) (0.000:0.000:0.000))
  )
 )

Every value is a triple of a minimum, a typical, and a maximum value in ns. Here, OpenSTA computes all three from the one typical-corner library: the minimum and the maximum from its minimum and maximum analyses, and the typical value as their mean.
IOPATH is the delay from an input pin to an output pin, first for a rising and then for a falling output. The clock-to-output delay of this flip-flop is about 0.16 ns.
TIMINGCHECK lists the limits that the flip-flop requires: the setup and hold times of D, the recovery and removal times of the asynchronous reset, and the minimum pulse widths. Section 6 explains them.
The delay of a wire would be an INTERCONNECT entry. Before the layout, these entries are all zero.

The wrapper fifo_sdf.sv instantiates the netlist and calls $sdf_annotate() at the start of the simulation. With GL=1 SDF=1, the runner uses it as the top level, compiles with -gspecify, which keeps the timing of the cell models, and passes the name of the SDF file as the run-time argument (plusarg) +SDF=...:


fifo/testbenches/cocotb/fifo_sdf.sv

// SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Simon Dorrer
// SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
// Description: Wrapper for the timing simulation of the synthesized
// FIFO. Icarus Verilog annotates the cell delays of the SDF file that
// the plusarg +SDF=<file> names.

`default_nettype none

module fifo_sdf (
  input  wire       clk_i,
  input  wire       rst_ni,
  input  wire       push_i,
  input  wire [7:0] data_i,
  input  wire       pop_i,
  output wire [7:0] data_o,
  output wire       full_o,
  output wire       empty_o
);

  fifo u_fifo (.*);

  string sdf_file;

  initial begin
    if ($value$plusargs("SDF=%s", sdf_file)) begin
      $sdf_annotate(sdf_file, u_fifo);
    end
  end

endmodule

`default_nettype wire


sta -no_init -exit syn/sta.tcl
cd testbenches/cocotb
GL=1 SDF=1 python3 fifo_tb.py
cd ../..
Both tests pass. Icarus Verilog prints 38 warnings SDF WARNING: ... TIMINGCHECK not supported, one per flip-flop. It reads the delays, but it never checks a setup, hold, recovery, or removal time. A timing violation therefore shows up in Icarus Verilog only if it makes a flip-flop capture a wrong value. Simulators that support timing checks evaluate the $setuphold and $recrem checks of the cell models, and on a violation the model of the flip-flop drives its output to x, the same mechanism that VITAL, the IEEE standard for ASIC cell models in VHDL, defines.
Four traps of the open-source flow, measured with OpenSTA 3.1.0 and Icarus Verilog 14.0. sta.tcl handles the first three:

OpenSTA writes the triples as (min::max), without the typical value, unless write_sdf gets the option -include_typ. Icarus Verilog annotates only the typical value, so without the option it annotates nothing, without any message. The simulation then runs without delays, while it seems to run with them. In the FIFO, empty_o falls 0.44 ns after the clock edge that stores the first push with the typical values, and 0 ns after it without them.
Icarus Verilog reports an error for the header lines VOLTAGE and TEMPERATURE, whose triples also lack the typical value.
Icarus Verilog annotates INTERCONNECT entries only with the option -ginterconnect, and even then not those that start at the bits of the input bus data_i. Before the layout, all wire delays are zero anyway, so sta.tcl removes all INTERCONNECT entries together with the two header lines. After the layout, the wire delays count, and the entries must stay.
Icarus Verilog does not support the state-dependent delays of the cell models, i.e., delays that depend on the values of the other inputs, e.g., the delay from the select input of a mux2_1 to its output, which depends on A0 and A1. These are the 68 sorry: ifnone with an edge-sensitive path is not supported messages. It uses the default delay of such a path instead.

The lesson of the first trap applies to every flow: zero error messages do not prove that the annotation worked. Check that a delay really shows up in the waveform.
A gate-level simulation is slower than an RTL simulation, because the netlist has more signals and events. For the small FIFO, the Python side of cocotb dominates: test_random, extended to 400 phases, i.e., 20,000 cycles, took about 1.0 s at RTL, 1.2 s at gate level, and 1.5 s with delays. For a large design, the difference grows with the number of cells, which is why only a selected set of tests runs on the netlist.






TipExercise: Timing Simulation Against Static Timing Analysis



All commands start in the folder content/verification/code/fifo. Synthesize the FIFO and write the SDF file as shown above.

Look at the report of sta -no_init -exit syn/sta.tcl. Which path is the critical one at 20 ns, and what limits its speed?
Find the shortest clock period at which static timing analysis reports no negative slack: CLK_PERIOD_NS=<period> sta -no_init -exit syn/sta.tcl. The delays in fifo.sdf do not depend on the clock period.
Find the shortest clock period at which the timing simulation still passes, e.g., with 2.2, 2.0, 1.8, and 1.7 ns (command below, in the folder testbenches/cocotb). Repeat it with other seeds.
Compare both results. Icarus Verilog checks no setup times. Is that the only reason why the timing simulation passes at clock periods for which static timing analysis reports violations? Which of the two do you trust for the tapeout?

export COCOTB_RANDOM_SEED=1
CLK_PERIOD_NS=2.2 GL=1 SDF=1 python3 fifo_tb.py


Before continuing, please finish the previous exercise. Once you are done, compare with the solution below.






TipSolution: Timing Simulation Against Static Timing Analysis






At 20 ns, the worst slack is 8.863 ns. The critical path starts at the input push_i, which the testbench changes at the falling edge, 10 ns after the rising one. It runs through an inverter and a nor4_1, which decodes the write enable of one storage entry and drives the select inputs of its eight multiplexers. Its rising output is slow (0.66 ns): it is pulled up through four PMOS transistors in series, and it drives this load. Through a mux2_1, the path then reaches the D input of a storage flip-flop 1.01 ns after the input change, and the flip-flop needs it 0.13 ns before the clock edge (setup time). Since this path has only half a period, the period must be at least twice 1.14 ns, i.e., 2.28 ns.
At 2.28 ns, the worst slack is 0.003 ns, and at 2.27 ns, it is -0.002 ns. The other paths are faster: the slowest output, full_o, settles 0.93 ns after the clock edge, and the slowest path between two flip-flops takes 1.75 ns plus the setup time.
The timing simulation passes at 2.2, 2.0, and 1.8 ns, with seeds 1 to 5. At 1.7 ns, it fails with every seed, already in the directed test: data_o = XXX1XXX1, expected 00010001. The first push misses the clock edge on exactly the critical path of step 1. In the simulation, the path takes 0.89 ns from the change of push_i to the falling outputs of the mux2_1 cells, but at 1.7 ns, the next rising edge comes after 0.85 ns. Entry 0 captures the 1-bits of 0x11, which arrive earlier through the faster rising outputs, keeps x in the other bits, and shows them until it is popped.
The timing simulation passes down to 1.8 ns, although static timing analysis requires 2.28 ns. The directed test does exercise the critical path, so the gap has three other causes, all in the simulator:

Icarus Verilog checks no setup times. A flip-flop takes its D input up to the clock edge, while static timing analysis requires it 0.13 ns earlier.
Icarus Verilog uses the typical value of each delay, while static timing analysis checks the setup time with the maximum values: 0.58 ns instead of 0.66 ns for the nor4_1.
Icarus Verilog ignores the state-dependent delays of the cell models and uses the default delay from the select input of the mux2_1 to its falling output: 0.25 ns instead of 0.29 ns.

Together, the path takes 0.06 + 0.58 + 0.25 ≈ 0.89 ns in the simulation, against 0.06 + 0.66 + 0.29 = 1.01 ns plus the setup time of 0.13 ns in static timing analysis. At 1.8 ns, the path arrives 10 ps before the clock edge. In general, a simulation sees a path at its slowest only if its stimulus causes exactly the slowest transitions, while static timing analysis covers every path without any stimulus. For the tapeout, trust static timing analysis. With a simulator that checks the timing limits, a timing simulation is a sanity check for what static timing analysis does not cover, e.g., the reset sequence and asynchronous inputs. With Icarus Verilog, it mainly catches wrong constraints and a missing annotation.

title: VLSI Design
text:
4.11 Regression and Continuous Integration
A design has many tests, and every change to the RTL can break any of them. A regression runs all tests with one command and reports one verdict. In the AMS chip template (Section 1.10), make sim-all runs all simulations of a macro, at RTL and at gate level, and make regression at the top level runs lint, the simulations, the FPGA build, and the LibreLane flow of the digital example macro and of the chip, with part of the DRC skipped to save run time. Continuous integration (CI) runs the regression automatically. The template runs make regression with GitHub Actions in the IIC-OSIC-TOOLS container every night at 02:00 UTC, and skips the run if nothing has changed since the last one.
A regression is only useful if a failing test fails the whole command. Section 2.6.2 showed that the cocotb runner does not set the exit status when a test fails, so the runner of every testbench must check results.xml with get_results(), as all testbenches of this course do. Some more rules for a useful regression:

Run the fast tests on every change, i.e., lint and the RTL tests. Run the slow ones every night, i.e., the gate-level and timing simulations and the complete flow.
Use fixed seeds in the regression, so that every failure can be reproduced, and run additional random seeds every night to explore new stimuli. Always log the seed.
Keep the regression green. A known failure hides every new one behind it.
Turn every bug that you find into a directed test of its scenario, so that it cannot come back unnoticed.

title: VLSI Design
text:
4.12 Further Reading

(Spear and Tumbush 2012) introduces the verification features of SystemVerilog: classes, constrained randomization, assertions, and functional coverage.
(Bergeron 2006) covers the methodology behind testbench architectures, coverage-driven verification, and verification plans.
The documentation of cocotb (cocotb developers 2026) describes the triggers, the runner, and the handling of signal values in detail.

title: VLSI Design
text:
4.13 Summary

Verification checks a design against its specification before the tapeout. Simulation works for every design at every level, but it can only show that a bug exists, never that none is left.
A verification plan gives each feature of the specification a check and a coverage goal. The verification is complete when all checks pass and all goals are reached.
A testbench separates the generator, the driver, the monitor, an independent reference model, the scoreboard, and the coverage collector. In cocotb, they are plain Python coroutines and classes, and the monitor samples after the driver, in the ReadOnly() phase of the falling edge.
Exhaustive tests are possible only for small combinational blocks and small parameter values. Constrained-random tests with a logged seed, combined with directed corner values, cover the rest.
Code coverage measures the RTL, and functional coverage measures the situations of the specification. The directed FIFO test reached 100 % line, branch, and expression coverage, but only 5 of 12 functional bins.
Coverage measures the stimuli, and mutation testing measures the checks. A surviving mutant points to a hole in the testbench or is equivalent.
Keep concurrent assertions in a separate checker attached with bind, which Verilator runs. Icarus Verilog and Yosys do not support them. Keep the checks at the ports in the cocotb testbench, so that they also run on the netlist.
The same testbench runs on the netlist, without and with the delays of an SDF file. Icarus Verilog annotates only the typical value of each delay, ignores state-dependent delays, and checks no setup or hold times, so a timing simulation is optimistic and does not replace static timing analysis.
A regression runs all tests with one command and fails if any test fails, on every change and every night.

In Section 5, we look inside the synthesis step that produced the netlist of this chapter: the standard-cell library, its timing model, and the logic equivalence check that proves the netlist equivalent to the RTL without any simulation.

title: VLSI Design
text:
5.1 Learning Objectives
After this chapter, you will be able to:

describe the steps of logic synthesis from the RTL to a netlist of standard cells, and name the Yosys commands behind them
explain what a standard cell is, how cells form rows, and which views of a library each tool of the flow reads
read a Liberty file: units, cell area, pin function, timing arcs with their timing sense, and the delay and power tables
compute the delay and the output slew of a cell by interpolation in its table, and check the result with OpenSTA
explain process, voltage, and temperature corners, and pick the corner for a timing check
trade area against speed in technology mapping
explain what logic equivalence checking proves, how it matches the two designs, where it can fail falsely, and run it with EQY

title: VLSI Design
text:
5.2 What Logic Synthesis Does
Logic synthesis translates the RTL into a netlist of standard cells that implements the same function, guided by goals for area and speed. Yosys does it in four steps (Figure 18):

Elaboration parses the RTL, builds the module hierarchy, and turns every process into a netlist of word-level cells: adders, comparators, multiplexers, and registers of any width. always_ff becomes a register cell, and always_comb becomes multiplexers and logic.
Optimization works on these word-level cells. It removes constant and unused logic, detects and re-encodes state machines (fsm), shares arithmetic between exclusive cases (share), and recognizes memories (memory).
Lowering breaks the word-level cells into generic gates and flip-flops of single bits, e.g., an 8-bit adder into its full adders, and optimizes them as a Boolean network. Yosys uses ABC (Brayton and Mishchenko 2010) for this, a tool for logic optimization from UC Berkeley.
Technology mapping replaces the generic gates by cells of the target library: dfflibmap the flip-flops, and ABC the logic, now with the function, area, and delay of every cell from the Liberty file.









Figure 18: The steps of logic synthesis with Yosys. Elaboration turns the RTL into a netlist of word-level cells, such as adders, multiplexers, and registers. The optimization works on these cells, e.g., it detects state machines and shares arithmetic. The lowering step breaks them down into generic single-bit gates and flip-flops, and the technology mapping finally replaces those by standard cells of the library. Only the last step needs the Liberty file. Yosys names its own cells with a dollar sign, e.g., $add and $mux at the word level and $_AND_ and $_DFF_PN0_ at the gate level.





The command synth runs the first three steps. Its script, printed by yosys -p "help synth", has four stages: begin builds the hierarchy, coarse elaborates and optimizes the word-level netlist, fine lowers it to gates, and check prints the statistics. dfflibmap and abc -liberty, which follow synth in all our scripts, are the fourth step.
The multiplexer of Section 2.5.4 shows the difference between the steps. After synth alone, its eight 4:1 multiplexers and the zero flag become 67 generic gates: 40 NAND, 20 AND, 5 NOR, and 2 AND-NOT gates. After the technology mapping, they become 11 standard cells with an area of 335.7 µm²: 8 mux4_1, 2 nor4_1, and one and2_1. ABC recognized that the library has a 4:1 multiplexer cell and used it, because it is smaller and faster than the gates it replaces.
cd /foss/designs/vlsi-design/content/sv_crashcourse/code/mux4
yosys -p "read_verilog -sv rtl/mux4.sv; synth -top mux4; stat"
yosys -p "read_verilog -sv rtl/mux4.sv; synth -top mux4; \
  dfflibmap -liberty $LIB; abc -liberty $LIB; opt_clean; \
  stat -liberty $LIB"

title: VLSI Design
text:
5.3 The Standard-Cell Library
A standard cell is a small, pre-designed layout of one logic function, e.g., an inverter, a NAND gate, or a flip-flop. All cells of a library have the same height, and their widths are multiples of one site. In SG13CMOS5L, every cell is 3.78 µm high, and a site is 0.48 µm wide. The layout tool places the cells side by side in rows, where they abut and share the supply rails VDD and VSS along their top and bottom edges (Figure 19). Every second row is flipped, so that neighboring rows share a rail. This regular structure is what makes automatic placement and routing of millions of cells possible.








Figure 19: Two rows of SG13CMOS5L standard cells, drawn to scale. Every cell is 3.78 µm high, and its width is a multiple of the 0.48 µm site. The cells of a row abut each other and share the supply rails VDD and VSS at their top and bottom edges. Every second row is flipped, so that two neighboring rows share one rail. Fill cells close the gaps, and decap cells add capacitance between the rails.





The cell names follow the pattern sg13cmos5l_<function>_<drive>. The function is a short name, e.g., inv, nand2, a21oi for an AND-OR-invert gate with a 2-input AND, mux4, or dfrbpq for a D flip-flop with an active-low reset and only a Q output. The drive strength scales the width of the transistors: a stronger cell such as inv_4 drives a larger load at the same delay, and needs more area and input capacitance for it. The library has 84 cells (Table 28).



Table 28: The 84 cells of the SG13CMOS5L standard-cell library

The physical cells have no logic function. Fill cells close the gaps in a row, so that the wells and rails continue. Decap cells add capacitance between VDD and VSS to stabilize the supply, and the antenna diode protects transistor gates against charge collected during fabrication (Section 10).

5.3.1 Library Views
Each tool of the flow needs a different description of the same cells, called a view. The PDK keeps them in $PDK_ROOT/ihp-sg13cmos5l/libs.ref/sg13cmos5l_stdcell (Table 29).
