title: VLSI Design
text:
7.7 Clock Gating
A register that keeps its value most of the time still consumes clock power in every cycle. SG13CMOS5L has no flip-flop with an enable (Section 3.4.3), so synthesis builds a register with an enable from a multiplexer in front of each flip-flop, which feeds back Q while the enable is low (Figure 28 (a)). Clock gating switches off the clock of the whole register instead, with one gate for all its flip-flops and without multiplexers (Figure 28 (b)).








Figure 28: Two ways to build a register with an enable, shown for one bit. (a) A multiplexer in front of each flip-flop feeds back Q while en is low, and the flip-flop is clocked in every cycle. (b) An integrated clock gate (ICG), here sg13cmos5l_lgcp_1, switches off the clock of the whole register while en is low. Its latch is transparent while clk is low, so a change of en reaches the AND gate only while clk is low, and gclk has only complete pulses.





A plain AND gate of clock and enable does not work (Figure 29). The enable comes from a register on the same clock, so it changes shortly after the rising edge, while the clock is high, and the AND gate passes the change at once. A rising enable produces a late clock edge, a falling one a short pulse, which clocks the register at the wrong time or violates the minimum pulse width of its flip-flops (Section 6.3).








Figure 29: Gating the clock with a plain AND gate and with an integrated clock gate. The enable en comes from a register on the same clock, so it changes shortly after the rising edges (dashed), while clk is high. The AND gate passes these changes to its output: a late edge in the second period and a short pulse in the fourth. The latch of the ICG passes en only while clk is low, so the gated clock has only complete pulses, at the third and the fourth edge.





An integrated clock gate (ICG) puts a latch, transparent while the clock is low, in front of the AND gate. The enable reaches the AND gate only during the low phase and stays stable while the clock is high, so the gated clock has only complete pulses. A flip-flop on the falling edge in place of the latch would give clean pulses as well, but the enable would have to arrive by the falling edge, i.e., within half a period. The latch accepts it until the rising edge. In SG13CMOS5L, the ICG is lgcp_1 with the pins GATE, CLK, and GCLK and an area of 27.2 µm², and its Liberty file marks it with clock_gating_integrated_cell : "latch_posedge". Its sibling slgcp_1 has an additional input SCE, which switches the clock on during the scan test (Section 9).
The clock passes through the ICG from CLK to GCLK, so STA times the gated flip-flops with the clock of the ICG. The path of the enable ends at the pin GATE, where the library defines a clock gating check, a setup and a hold check against the rising edge of CLK. Like the data input of a flip-flop, the enable must be stable shortly before the rising edge. The ICG also delays the clock of the gated flip-flops, which clock tree synthesis balances against the other flip-flops (Section 10).
Yosys inserts the ICGs with the pass clockgate, between synth and dfflibmap. It replaces each group of flip-flops that share a clock and an enable by one ICG and flip-flops without enable:
clockgate -pos sg13cmos5l_lgcp_1 GATE:CLK:GCLK -min_net_size 4
-pos names the ICG for flip-flops on the rising edge and its pins for the enable, the clock, and the gated clock. -min_net_size sets the smallest group that gets an ICG, since an ICG is clocked in every cycle and costs area and power of its own. LibreLane runs the same pass when SYNTH_CLOCKGATE_MIN_WIDTH is set, and it inserts ICGs when SYNTH_CLOCKGATE_POSEDGE_ICG names the cell, e.g., sg13cmos5l_lgcp_1/GATE/CLK/GCLK. The configuration of SG13CMOS5L sets neither and even excludes lgcp_1 and slgcp_1 from synthesis, so LibreLane gates no clocks unless a design configures it.






TipExercise: Gate the Clock



All commands start in the folder content/synth_opt/code/clock_gate. The module rtl/cg_reg.sv is a 32-bit register with the enable en_i. The testbench tb/tb_cg_reg.sv simulates its netlist for 1600 clock cycles at 250 MHz, applies new random data in every cycle, sets en_i high in one of EVERY cycles (default 16), compares the output with a model, and writes the activity of every net into cg_reg.vcd.

Draw clk, en_i, the latched enable, and GCLK of the ICG in the style of Figure 29, for an enable that a flip-flop on clk sets high for exactly one cycle. At which rising edge do the gated flip-flops load data_i, and is it the same edge as in the version with multiplexers?
Synthesize cg_reg without clock gating:
cd /foss/designs/vlsi-design/content/synth_opt/code/clock_gate
yosys -p "read_verilog -sv rtl/cg_reg.sv; synth -top cg_reg; \
  dfflibmap -liberty $LIB; abc -constr $CONSTR -liberty $LIB; \
  opt_clean; stat -liberty $LIB; write_verilog -noattr cg_reg.nl.v"
Which cells does the netlist have? Simulate the netlist with the models of the cells, and run the power analysis with the activity of the simulation:
CELLS=$PDK_ROOT/ihp-sg13cmos5l/libs.ref/sg13cmos5l_stdcell/verilog
iverilog -g2012 -gno-specify -o sim.vvp $CELLS/sg13cmos5l_udp.v \
  $CELLS/sg13cmos5l_stdcell.v cg_reg.nl.v tb/tb_cg_reg.sv
vvp -n sim.vvp
TOP=cg_reg VCD=cg_reg.vcd sta -no_init -exit ../syn/power.tcl
Icarus Verilog prints the 68 sorry messages of Section 4.10.2, which do not matter without delays. How much power does the register consume? Is the share of the flip-flops larger or smaller than in bs_reg, and why? Which cells besides the flip-flops and the multiplexers does the netlist have, and why?
Insert clockgate -pos sg13cmos5l_lgcp_1 GATE:CLK:GCLK -min_net_size 4; after synth -top cg_reg; and repeat step 2. Compare the cells, the area, and the power. What consumes the power that remains?
Repeat steps 2 and 3 with the enable high in every cycle, i.e., with -P tb_cg_reg.EVERY=1 added to the iverilog command. Compare again. Which entry of the reports makes the comparison unfair, and by how much?



Before continuing, please finish the previous exercise. Once you are done, compare with the solution below.






TipSolution: Gate the Clock






The flip-flop sets en_i shortly after a rising edge, call it edge 1, and clears it shortly after edge 2. The latch passes the high enable during the low phase after edge 1 and holds it while clk is high after edge 2, so GCLK has exactly one complete pulse, at edge 2. During the low phase after edge 2, the latch passes the low enable, and the pulse at edge 3 is suppressed. The gated flip-flops load data_i at edge 2, the same edge at which the version with multiplexers loads it, since its flip-flops sample en_i = 1 at edge 2.
The netlist has 67 cells and 2223 µm²: 32 dfrbpq_1, 32 multiplexers (30 mux2_1, 2 mux2_2), and 3 buf_8, which drive the enable to the 32 select inputs. The simulation reports 1600 cycles, en_i in 1 of 16, 0 errors, and OpenSTA annotates the activity of all 329 pins. The register consumes 490 µW, 474 µW of it in the flip-flops (97 %, almost all internal power) and 16 µW in the multiplexers and buffers. The share of the flip-flops is larger than the 67 % in bs_reg, because the register has no logic besides the multiplexers. It changes in only one of 16 cycles, but its flip-flops are clocked in every cycle.
With clockgate, the netlist has 33 cells and 1595 µm², 28 % less: 32 dfrbpq_1 and one lgcp_1, and no multiplexers. The simulation passes again. The power drops to 89.6 µW, 82 % less: 82.5 µW in the flip-flops and 7.1 µW in the group Clock, i.e., 4.8 µW of internal power in the ICG and 2.3 µW for switching the gated clock net. Of the power in the flip-flops, the clock edges in one of 16 cycles cause only a part. Without the multiplexers, the new random data reaches the D pins in every cycle, which costs internal power in the flip-flops even without a clock edge: the Liberty file gives the pin D of dfrbpq_1 an internal power of its own. With data that changes only together with the enable, i.e., with data = $urandom only in the cycles in which the testbench sets en, the flip-flops of the gated register consume 39.6 µW.
With the enable high in every cycle, the register without clock gating consumes 673 µW (631 µW in the flip-flops, 41 µW in the multiplexers), and the one with clock gating 665 µW (621 µW in the flip-flops, 43.9 µW in the group Clock). The group Clock of the gated register includes 36.4 µW for switching the gated clock net with its 32 clock pins. The register without clock gating has the same net, but its driver is the input port clk_i, which belongs to no cell, so OpenSTA charges its power nowhere. The gated register has such a net as well, from clk_i to the pin CLK of the ICG, but with its 4.9 fF, it costs only about 1.8 µW. Compared fairly, the register without clock gating needs about 709 µW and the one with clock gating about 667 µW, so the ICG still saves about 6 %, because it replaces the multiplexers. With the enable in one of 16 cycles, the fair comparison is 527 µW against 91 µW. For a register of a few bits, however, an ICG that is clocked in every cycle may cost more than it saves, which is what -min_net_size is for.

title: VLSI Design
text:
7.8 Summary

Synthesis optimizes the operators (Yosys) and the gates (ABC) of a design, but not its architecture: it keeps the latency and the algorithm of the RTL, and, apart from retiming on request, its registers. Pipelines, parallelism, and the choice of the algorithm remain the job of the designer.
A ripple-carry adder is small and slow, a parallel-prefix adder computes the carries in a tree of \(\log_2 n\) to \(2 \log_2 n - 1\) levels. Yosys builds a Brent-Kung adder by default and others on request. The default scripts of ABC rewrite for area and flatten the prefix trees. A script that keeps the structure keeps the architecture, and a delay-oriented script restructures even a ripple-carry adder into a few levels of wide gates, at the price of area.
Operations that are never needed in the same cycle can share an operator. Yosys 0.70 shares multipliers only without alumacc, so write the sharing into the RTL where it matters, and check the result with stat.
A pipeline register shortens the critical path and raises the throughput, at the cost of latency, registers, and a fixed overhead per stage. Retiming moves registers across logic, but in the open-source flow only flip-flops without reset.
CMOS circuits consume switching, internal, and leakage power. Dynamic power grows with \(a C V^2 f\), so the supply voltage is the strongest lever, and the activity the one that the design controls. In synchronous designs, the flip-flops and the clock take a large share, and a power analysis before clock tree synthesis does not see the clock tree.
OpenSTA estimates power from the Liberty file and the activity of every net, which comes from a default assumption or from the VCD file of a simulation.
Clock gating switches off the clock of idle registers. It needs an integrated clock gate whose latch keeps the enable stable while the clock is high. Yosys inserts it with clockgate, and on a 32-bit register with an enable in one of 16 cycles, it saves more than 80 % of the power and 28 % of the area.

In Section 8, the designs get more than one clock, and we see how signals cross safely from one clock domain to another.

title: VLSI Design
text:
8.1 Learning Objectives
After this chapter, you will be able to:

tell synchronous from asynchronous clocks, and find the clock domain crossings of a design
explain metastability, measure the time constant of a flip-flop, and compute the mean time between failures of a synchronizer
synchronize a level and a pulse into another clock domain
explain why a bus whose bits can change at the same time cannot cross through one synchronizer per bit, and cross it with Gray code, a handshake, or an asynchronous FIFO
simulate clock domain crossings with metastability injection
constrain clock domain crossings in SDC
release an asynchronous reset synchronously with a reset synchronizer

title: VLSI Design
text:
8.2 Clock Domains
A clock domain is the set of registers that one clock drives. Two clocks are synchronous if they come from the same source with a known phase relation, e.g., a clock and the clock divided from it by a counter. Once the constraints define the derived clock with create_generated_clock, STA knows their edges and times the paths between them like any other path (Section 6.8). Two clocks are asynchronous if they come from different sources, e.g., two crystal oscillators, or if their phase relation is unknown. Their phase drifts, so a signal from domain A reaches the registers of domain B at an arbitrary moment relative to clk_b. An asynchronous input from a pin is a crossing as well: a button, a sensor, or a chip outside on its own clock runs in a domain of its own. An input that comes from a register on the same clock, as in the constraints of Section 6.6, is timed with set_input_delay instead.
A clock domain crossing (CDC) is a path that starts at a register of one domain and ends at a register of another. Inside a synchronous design, the setup and hold checks of Section 6.5 guarantee that no flip-flop ever sees its data change inside its window. At a crossing between asynchronous clocks, no check can guarantee that, and every crossing violates the window from time to time.

title: VLSI Design
text:
8.3 Metastability
The master latch of a flip-flop (Section 6.2) stores its value in two cross-coupled inverters. This loop has two stable states, 0 and 1, and an unstable balance point in between, like a ball on the top of a hill. If D changes just at the moment the master closes, the loop starts close to the balance point, and the flip-flop is metastable. The small voltage difference grows exponentially, with a time constant \(\tau\) of the loop, until the loop reaches 0 or 1. The closer the data edge was to the critical moment, the smaller the start difference and the longer it takes. Meanwhile, the output may show a voltage between 0 and 1 or switch late, and two flip-flops behind it may see different values.
The script meta/dff_meta.py measures this with ngspice on the transistor netlist of dfrbpq_1 from the PDK (libs.ref/sg13cmos5l_stdcell/spice/sg13cmos5l_stdcell.spice), with a load of 5 fF and edges of 0.15 ns. It moves a rising D toward the rising clock edge and finds, by bisection to \(10^{-19}\) s, the latest arrival that the flip-flop still captures. Then it moves the data edge away from that critical point by \(\delta\), decade by decade, and measures the clock-to-output delay. The netlist of the PDK is the schematic of the cell, without the wiring capacitance of its layout, so the script adds an estimated 1.5 fF to each of its 15 internal nodes:
cd /foss/designs/vlsi-design/content/cdc/code/meta
python3 dff_meta.py








Figure 30: Clock-to-output delay of sg13cmos5l_dfrbpq_1 in ngspice, typical corner, with 1.5 fF at each internal node, over the time \(\delta\) by which the rising D arrives before the latest arrival that the flip-flop still captures. Every decade closer to that point adds about 198 ps, i.e., \(\tau \ln 10\) with \(\tau\) = 85.9 ps. Far from the point, the delay approaches its normal value \(t_\text{cq0}\) = 220.4 ps. The line is the fit from \(10^{-17}\) to \(10^{-14}\) s.





Figure 30 shows the result. Without metastability, the clock-to-output delay is \(t_\text{cq0}\) = 220.4 ps. Near the critical point, every decade adds about 198 ps. The delay follows
\[t_\text{cq} = t_\text{cq0} + \tau \ln \frac{T_0}{2\delta},\]
with \(\tau\) = 85.9 ps and \(T_0\) = 23.5 ps from a fit from \(10^{-17}\) to \(10^{-14}\) s. Farther from the point, the start difference of the latch is no longer small, and the delay approaches its normal value. How good is the estimate of the wiring capacitance? The library gives a clock-to-output delay of 0.202 ns for the same edges, whose slew from 20 to 80 % is 0.09 ns, and the same load, a little less than the 0.207 ns of Table 32 at slews of 0.1 ns. With the estimate, \(t_\text{cq0}\) is 9 % higher, and the bare schematic (CPAR=0 python3 dff_meta.py) gives 190.1 ps, 6 % lower, with \(\tau\) = 62.0 ps and \(T_0\) = 17.0 ps. The real \(\tau\) lies between the two, and the estimate errs on the safe side. Only a netlist extracted from the layout of the cell would give it exactly. Data that arrives by \(\delta\) after the critical point behaves about the same way, mirrored: the master latch needs about as long to resolve, but to the old value. So the flip-flop needs more than an additional time \(t_r\) whenever the data edge falls into a window of width \(T_0 e^{-t_r/\tau}\) around the critical point. To resolve within 1 ns more than \(t_\text{cq0}\), the data edge must miss a window of only \(2.1 \cdot 10^{-16}\) s, in which light travels 62 nm. But it will hit it sooner or later.
How often? Data that changes \(f_\text{data}\) times per second, sampled at \(f_\text{clk}\), hits the window with the probability \(T_0 e^{-t_r/\tau} f_\text{clk}\) per change. If the flip-flop has the time \(t_r\) to resolve before the next flip-flop samples it, the resolution time, the mean time between failures is
\[\text{MTBF} = \frac{e^{t_r/\tau}}{T_0 \, f_\text{clk} \, f_\text{data}}.\]
\(T_0\) and \(\tau\) are properties of the flip-flop and its corner, which a circuit simulation or a measurement gives. \(T_0\) is a parameter of the law above, not the setup time of the library. The time \(t_r\) is what remains of the period after the normal clock-to-output delay, the logic behind the flip-flop, and the setup time of the next one: \(t_r = T - t_\text{cq0} - t_\text{logic} - t_\text{su}\). It sits in the exponent, so a few hundred picoseconds more or less change the MTBF by orders of magnitude.

title: VLSI Design
VLSI Design
text:
8.5 Crossing with Several Bits
A bus whose bits can change at the same time cannot cross through one synchronizer per bit. Each bit resolves on its own, so when several bits change at the same time, the destination can see a mix of old and new bits for a cycle, a value that the source never sent. A binary counter that steps from 7 to 8, i.e., from 0111 to 1000, changes all four bits and may arrive as any value from 0 to 15. There are three ways out:

Gray code for counters and pointers. Consecutive values differ in exactly one bit, so the destination sees either the old or the new value, never a mix. The Gray code of a binary value \(b\) is \(g = b \oplus (b \gg 1)\), i.e., 000, 001, 011, 010, 110, 111, 101, 100 for 0 to 7, and back to binary, bit \(i\) is the XOR of all bits of \(g\) from bit \(i\) upward.
A handshake for data words that change rarely. The source puts the word on the bus, keeps it stable, and toggles a request, which crosses through a synchronizer. When the destination sees the request, the word has been stable for several cycles, and the destination captures it and toggles an acknowledge back. The source changes the word only after the acknowledge has come back. Only the two control bits cross through synchronizers, at the price of several cycles per word.
An asynchronous FIFO for data streams (Section 8.6).

An RTL simulation cannot show these problems by itself, because metastability is an analog effect that an RTL simulator does not model. The model sync/sim/sync_2ff_meta.sv replaces sync/rtl/sync_2ff.sv in a testbench. It has the same module name and ports, and it injects metastability: a bit of d_i that changed less than 1 ns before the clock edge resolves randomly to its old or its new value. The window is far wider than the real one, so that a crossing bug shows up within a few thousand cycles instead of years. At the end of a simulation, the model reports in how many samples at least one bit took its old value.






TipExercise: Count Across Clock Domains



All commands start in the folder content/cdc/code/gray. The module rtl/cnt_cross_bin.sv has a 4-bit counter in domain A that increments in every cycle, and reads it in domain B through one synchronizer per bit. The testbench tb/tb_cnt_cross.sv runs domain A at 10 ns and domain B at 13.7 ns for 5000 cycles of domain B, and it reports an error whenever the count in domain B advances by more than 2 in a cycle. The folder holds the reference solution rtl/cnt_cross_gray.sv, so move it out of the way first: cd /foss/designs/vlsi-design/content/cdc/code/gray, then mv rtl/cnt_cross_gray.sv cnt_cross_gray_solution.sv.

Simulate cnt_cross_bin with ../sync/rtl/sync_2ff.sv and with the model:
iverilog -g2012 -DDUT=cnt_cross_bin -o sim.vvp \
  rtl/cnt_cross_bin.sv ../sync/rtl/sync_2ff.sv tb/tb_cnt_cross.sv
vvp -n sim.vvp
iverilog -g2012 -DDUT=cnt_cross_bin -o sim.vvp \
  rtl/cnt_cross_bin.sv ../sync/sim/sync_2ff_meta.sv \
  tb/tb_cnt_cross.sv
vvp -n sim.vvp
How many errors does each run report, and in how many samples does the model report a bit at its old value? For the first two wrong counts of the second run, find the counter step that FF1 sampled, and which bits took their old and which their new value. Hint: the count advances by 1 or 2 per cycle of domain B.
Draw a block diagram of a counter that crosses in Gray code: the counter and the conversion to Gray code in domain A, the synchronizers, and the conversion back in domain B. Which signals are registers?
Write rtl/cnt_cross_gray.sv with the ports of cnt_cross_bin, check it with verilator --lint-only -Wall rtl/cnt_cross_gray.sv ../sync/rtl/sync_2ff.sv, and simulate it with the model, i.e., the second iverilog command of step 1 with -DDUT=cnt_cross_gray and rtl/cnt_cross_gray.sv. How many errors remain?



Before continuing, please finish the previous exercise. Once you are done, compare with the solution below.






TipSolution: Count Across Clock Domains






With rtl/sync_2ff.sv, the testbench reports 5000 cycles of domain B, 0 errors. In an RTL simulation, every bit that changes at an edge of clk_a is sampled consistently by the next edge of clk_b, so the binary crossing looks correct. With the model, it reports 224 errors, and in 334 of 5001 samples, at least one bit took its old value. The first wrong counts are 7 after 4 at 90.0 ns, 12 after 14 at 350.4 ns, and 1 after 12 at 364.1 ns. One cycle of domain B earlier, at 335.65 ns, FF1 sampled the counter 0.65 ns after it had stepped from 15 (1111) to 0 (0000), and all four bits changed. The two upper bits resolved to their old, the two lower ones to their new value, 1100, i.e., 12, a value the counter had four counts earlier. The count 1 at 364.1 ns is correct again, but it is flagged because it follows the wrong 12. At 90.0 ns, the step from 5 (0101) to 6 (0110) arrived as 0111, i.e., 7: bit 0 kept its old 1, and bit 1 took its new 1.
In domain A, the counter cnt_a_q and a register gray_a_q that holds its Gray code. The register is the source of the synchronizers, so the XOR gates in front of it cannot reach domain B with a glitch. In domain B, the four synchronizers and the combinational conversion back to binary behind them. The Gray register delays the count by one cycle of domain A, which does not matter for a counter that crosses domains.
The reference solution:



gray/rtl/cnt_cross_gray.sv

// SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Simon Dorrer
// SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
// Description: The counter of cnt_cross_bin, crossing in Gray code.
// Only one bit changes per count, so domain B sees either the old or
// the new value, never a mix.

`default_nettype none

module cnt_cross_gray #(
  parameter int unsigned W = 4
) (
  input  logic         clk_a_i,
  input  logic         rst_a_ni,
  input  logic         clk_b_i,
  input  logic         rst_b_ni,
  output logic [W-1:0] cnt_b_o
);

  logic [W-1:0] cnt_a_q, gray_a_q, gray_b;

  // Domain A: the counter and its Gray code in a register, so that
  // no logic glitch reaches the synchronizer
  always_ff @(posedge clk_a_i or negedge rst_a_ni) begin
    if (!rst_a_ni) begin
      cnt_a_q  <= '0;
      gray_a_q <= '0;
    end else begin
      cnt_a_q  <= cnt_a_q + 1'b1;
      gray_a_q <= cnt_a_q ^ (cnt_a_q >> 1);
    end
  end

  // Into domain B, then back to binary
  sync_2ff #(.WIDTH(W)) u_sync (
    .clk_i (clk_b_i),
    .rst_ni(rst_b_ni),
    .d_i   (gray_a_q),
    .q_o   (gray_b)
  );

  always_comb begin
    for (int i = 0; i < W; i++) begin
      cnt_b_o[i] = ^(gray_b >> i);
    end
  end

endmodule

`default_nettype wire


With the model, no error remains in 5000 cycles, although a bit took its old value in 260 samples. Each of them is one bit of a Gray step, so the count is the old or the new value, which the testbench accepts.

title: VLSI Design
VLSI Design
text:
8.7 Constraints for Clock Domain Crossings
The constraints of async_fifo define one clock per domain, and the ports of each domain refer to their own clock:


fifo/syn/async_fifo.sdc

# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Simon Dorrer
# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
# Description: Timing constraints of async_fifo: a write clock of
# 100 MHz and an unrelated read clock of about 70 MHz, each with the
# ports of its own domain.

create_clock -name wclk -period 10.0 [get_ports wclk_i]
create_clock -name rclk -period 14.3 [get_ports rclk_i]
set_clock_transition 0.1 [all_clocks]
set_clock_uncertainty 0.1 [all_clocks]

# The ports of each domain refer to their own clock
set w_in [get_ports {wrst_ni push_i data_i*}]
set r_in [get_ports {rrst_ni pop_i}]
set_input_delay 1.0 -clock wclk $w_in
set_input_delay 1.0 -clock rclk $r_in
set_output_delay 1.0 -clock wclk [get_ports full_o]
set_output_delay 1.0 -clock rclk [get_ports {data_o* empty_o}]
set_driving_cell -lib_cell sg13cmos5l_buf_2 -pin X $w_in
set_driving_cell -lib_cell sg13cmos5l_buf_2 -pin X $r_in
set_load 0.01 [all_outputs]


Without further constraints, STA treats two clocks as synchronous. It searches the edges of both clocks over their common period, here 1430 ns, for the tightest pair. Synthesized as in the earlier chapters (134 cells, 3979 µm²), async_fifo gives this report:
cd /foss/designs/vlsi-design/content/cdc/code/fifo
yosys -p "read_verilog -sv ../sync/rtl/sync_2ff.sv \
  rtl/async_fifo.sv; synth -top async_fifo; flatten; \
  dfflibmap -liberty $LIB; abc -constr $CONSTR -liberty $LIB; \
  opt_clean; stat -liberty $LIB; \
  write_verilog -noattr async_fifo.nl.v"
sta -no_init -exit syn/sta.tcl
The worst path of the group rclk runs from a memory flip-flop, launched by wclk at 100.0 ns, to data_o[0], captured by rclk at 100.1 ns, and fails with a slack of -1.414 ns. The worst path of the group wclk ends at a synchronizer flip-flop of the read pointer and fails with -0.382 ns. Both are meaningless: the clocks have no fixed phase, the edges come arbitrarily close to each other anyway, and the synchronizers and the protocol of the FIFO take care of it.
set_clock_groups -asynchronous tells STA that the clocks are unrelated, and it then times no path between them:
set_clock_groups -asynchronous -group wclk -group rclk
With CDC=1 sta -no_init -exit syn/sta.tcl, the script adds this line, the crossing paths disappear (No paths found), and the worst slacks are 12.488 ns in rclk and 8.171 ns in wclk. The constraint hides every crossing, including one without a synchronizer, so STA cannot check crossings at all. Commercial CDC tools check the structure of every crossing. In the open-source flow, design rules do the job: every crossing goes through one of a few synchronizer modules, such as sync_2ff. A search for their instances finds the synchronizers, but not a crossing without one. For that, list the endpoints of all crossing paths before the clock groups hide them:
report_checks -from [get_clocks wclk] -to [get_clocks rclk] \
  -group_path_count 100 -endpoint_path_count 1 -format end
Together with the other direction, async_fifo has 14 such endpoints: the 8 outputs data_o, which the protocol of the FIFO protects, and the 6 first flip-flops of the two synchronizers. Any other endpoint would be a crossing without a synchronizer.
A stricter alternative limits the delay of every crossing path instead of removing it, so that the bits of a Gray pointer arrive within one period of their source clock of each other, and the memory data within less than a read period, before the read domain can use the entry:
set_max_delay 10.0 -ignore_clock_latency \
  -from [get_clocks wclk] -to [get_clocks rclk]
set_max_delay 10.0 -ignore_clock_latency \
  -from [get_clocks rclk] -to [get_clocks wclk]
set_false_path -hold -from [get_clocks wclk] -to [get_clocks rclk]
set_false_path -hold -from [get_clocks rclk] -to [get_clocks wclk]
The limit of 10 ns is the period of the write clock, the source of the write pointer, which is the tighter case. -ignore_clock_latency leaves the clock latencies out of the limit, which after clock tree synthesis differ between the two unrelated clock trees, and it changes nothing for ideal clocks. With CDC=2 sta -no_init -exit syn/sta.tcl, the script uses these lines instead of the clock groups. OpenSTA reports the crossing paths in the path group path delay, the path to data_o[0] with a slack of 8.586 ns against the limit of 10 ns. Without the two false paths, it would still check hold between the clocks, which means as little as the setup checks before.

title: VLSI Design
text:
8.8 Resets
The asynchronous reset of our designs (Section 2.5.6) acts at once, without a clock. Asserting it at any moment is safe: every flip-flop goes into reset. Releasing it is a crossing. The reset comes from a pin or from a power-on-reset circuit, which holds the reset low until the supply has settled, asynchronous to the clock, and when its release falls into the window of the recovery and removal checks (Section 6.3), some flip-flops leave the reset at one clock edge and others one edge later. The design then starts in a state that the RTL never reaches.
A reset synchronizer asserts the reset of a clock domain at once, asynchronously, and releases it synchronously, at a clock edge. Its output drives the reset inputs of all registers of the domain, so that they all leave the reset at the same clock edge. Every clock domain needs its own reset synchronizer. The reset input itself must be free of glitches, because even a short pulse resets the design asynchronously. A chip therefore takes it from a power-on-reset circuit or from a filtered pin, whose input stage ignores pulses shorter than a set time.






TipExercise: Release the Reset



All commands start in the folder content/cdc/code/reset. It holds the reference solution rtl/rst_sync.sv, so move it out of the way first: cd /foss/designs/vlsi-design/content/cdc/code/reset, then mv rtl/rst_sync.sv rst_sync_solution.sv.

Draw the reset synchronizer with the ports clk_i, rst_ni, and rst_no, and a timing diagram of clk_i, rst_ni, the internal flip-flop, and rst_no for a reset that falls between two clock edges and rises shortly before a rising edge. Hint: start from sync_2ff. What must the first flip-flop load after the release?
Write rtl/rst_sync.sv, check it with verilator --lint-only -Wall rtl/rst_sync.sv, and simulate it with the testbench:
iverilog -g2012 -o sim.vvp rtl/rst_sync.sv tb/tb_rst_sync.sv
vvp -n sim.vvp
When does rst_no rise after the release, and how many errors does the testbench report?
The module rtl/bs_reg_rs.sv puts your synchronizer in front of the barrel shifter between two registers of Section 6.7. Synthesize it and run the timing script with the constraints of bs_reg (Section 6.6):
yosys -p "read_verilog -sv \
  ../../../verification/code/barrel_shift/rtl/barrel_shift.sv \
  ../../../sequential/code/bs_reg/rtl/bs_reg.sv \
  rtl/rst_sync.sv rtl/bs_reg_rs.sv; synth -top bs_reg_rs; \
  flatten; dfflibmap -liberty $LIB; \
  abc -constr $CONSTR -liberty $LIB; opt_clean; \
  stat -liberty $LIB; write_verilog -noattr bs_reg_rs.nl.v"
sta -no_init -exit syn/sta.tcl
What is the slack of the worst recovery path now? How long does its startpoint need to drive its load, compared with the clock-to-output delay in Table 32, and what does that do to the recovery time? Compare the minimum periods with those of bs_reg in Section 6.7. What does report_check_types report, and why did synthesis not fix it?
Which checks does STA still make on the input rst_ni, and do they mean anything? The script reports them at its end. Copy syn/bs_reg_rs.sdc to syn/bs_reg_rs_rst.sdc, add the constraint that fits, and run SDC=syn/bs_reg_rs_rst.sdc sta -no_init -exit syn/sta.tcl. Which checks remain in the group asynchronous, and does the minimum period change?



Before continuing, please finish the previous exercise. Once you are done, compare with the solution below.






TipSolution: Release the Reset






The circuit (Figure 33) and its timing (Figure 34):









Figure 33: The reset synchronizer: two flip-flops with an asynchronous reset. rst_ni resets both at once. After its release, the first flip-flop loads the constant 1 at the next rising edge of clk_i, possibly metastable, and the second one passes it on one period later, as rst_no for all registers of the clock domain.













Figure 34: Timing of the reset synchronizer. rst_ni falls between two clock edges, and meta_q and rst_no fall at once. rst_ni rises within the recovery time before a rising edge (dashed), so meta_q may become metastable (crossed). Here it settles to 1, and rst_no rises one period later. If it settled to 0, rst_no would rise one period later still, again at a clock edge for all registers of the domain.






The reference solution:



reset/rtl/rst_sync.sv

// SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Simon Dorrer
// SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
// Description: Reset synchronizer. Asserts the reset of a clock
// domain at once, asynchronously, and releases it synchronously, two
// or, if the first flip-flop resolves late, three rising edges of
// clk_i after rst_ni rises.

`default_nettype none

module rst_sync (
  input  logic clk_i,
  input  logic rst_ni,  // asynchronous reset, e.g., from a pad
  output logic rst_no   // reset of the clock domain of clk_i
);

  logic meta_q;  // may be metastable after the release

  always_ff @(posedge clk_i or negedge rst_ni) begin
    if (!rst_ni) begin
      meta_q <= 1'b0;
      rst_no <= 1'b0;
    end else begin
      meta_q <= 1'b1;
      rst_no <= meta_q;
    end
  end

endmodule

`default_nettype wire


The testbench prints that rst_no is low 0.1 ns after rst_ni falls at 42 ns, between two clock edges, and that after the release at 64.8 ns, 0.2 ns before the edge at 65 ns, rst_no rises at 75 ns, the second rising edge after the release, with 0 errors.

bs_reg_rs has 927 cells, 15,343 µm², and 73 flip-flops, two more than bs_reg. The worst recovery path now starts at the second flip-flop of the synchronizer, whose output drives the RESET_B pins of all 71 registers. The flip-flop needs 1.375 ns for that, against its normal 0.207 ns. The slew of 1.721 ns raises the recovery time to 0.451 ns, and the slack is 2.074 ns. The release of the reset is now a path between two registers of the same clock, and report_clock_min_period includes it: \(1.375 + 0.451 + 0.1 = 1.93\) ns (519 MHz), with and without the port paths. In bs_reg, the paths between the registers needed 1.69 ns, and the reset input with its input delay limited the block to 2.02 ns. report_check_types reports the output of the synchronizer flip-flop with 0.43 pF against a limit of 0.30 pF. The load lies beyond the last index of the tables, so the delay and the slew above are extrapolated (Section 5.5). ABC buffers only the logic it maps, and this net runs from a flip-flop straight to flip-flops. The layout flow buffers it like any net with a large fanout (Section 10).
STA still checks the recovery and the removal of the two synchronizer flip-flops against rst_ni with its input delay of 1 ns, with slacks of 2.768 and 1.007 ns. These checks mean nothing: the release of rst_ni is asynchronous, and violating the recovery time of the first flip-flop is exactly the case that the synchronizer handles. The second flip-flop loads the 0 of the first one at the first edge after the release, so its output is the same whether it leaves the reset at this edge or the next. The constraint is a false path:

set_false_path -from [get_ports rst_ni]
With it, STA finds no path from rst_ni anymore, the remaining checks of the group asynchronous all start at the synchronizer, with a worst removal slack of 1.341 ns, and the minimum period stays at 1.93 ns.

title: VLSI Design
text:
8.9 Summary

Registers driven by one clock form a clock domain. Paths between asynchronous clocks, and from asynchronous input pins such as a button or a chip on its own clock, cross domains, and STA cannot check them.
A flip-flop whose data changes inside its window becomes metastable and resolves with the time constant \(\tau\). In ngspice, with an estimate of its wiring capacitance, dfrbpq_1 has \(\tau\) = 85.9 ps and \(T_0\) = 23.5 ps in the typical corner. The MTBF \(e^{t_r/\tau}/(T_0 f_\text{clk} f_\text{data})\) depends exponentially on the resolution time, so design for the slow corner.
A two-flip-flop synchronizer gives the first flip-flop a period to resolve. It needs a register in the source domain, no logic between the flip-flops, and one synchronizer per signal. A third flip-flop multiplies the MTBF by about \(e^{(T - t_\text{cq0} - t_\text{su})/\tau}\). A pulse crosses as a toggled level.
A bus whose bits can change at the same time cannot cross through one synchronizer per bit. Counters and pointers cross in Gray code, rare data words with a handshake, data streams through an asynchronous FIFO with Gray pointers, whose flags may be pessimistic but are never low when the FIFO is full or empty.
RTL simulation does not show metastability. A synchronizer model with metastability injection makes crossing bugs visible.
STA needs set_clock_groups -asynchronous or set_max_delay -ignore_clock_latency for the paths between asynchronous clocks, and the structure of the crossings must be checked by review or a CDC tool.
A reset synchronizer asserts the reset asynchronously and releases it synchronously, one per clock domain, and the input reset is a false path.

In Section 9, the design gets scan chains, and the clock domains and synchronizers of this chapter need special care in test mode.

title: VLSI Design
text:
9.1 Learning Objectives
After this chapter, you will be able to:

explain why every manufactured die is tested, and relate yield, fault coverage, and defect level
model defects as stuck-at, transition, bridging, and stuck-open faults, and explain IDDQ testing
find a test for a fault by hand and with a SAT solver, and recognize untestable faults
explain how scan makes a sequential circuit testable, insert scan chains with OpenROAD, and compute the test time
generate test vectors with Fault and apply them through a scan chain in simulation
apply the design rules for testability to clocks, clock gates, resets, clock domains, and the scan chain itself
name the tests beyond scan: at-speed test, built-in self-test, and boundary scan

title: VLSI Design
text:
9.2 Why Test?
Manufacturing is never perfect. Particles on the wafer, defects in the lithography, and variations of the process cause shorts between wires, open vias, and transistors that do not switch. The share of good dies on a wafer is the yield \(Y\). It falls with the die area and rises as a process matures, but it never reaches 100 %, so every die must be tested before it is shipped. Verification asks whether the design is right, the test asks whether a die equals the design (Section 4.2). The test assumes that the design is correct, and it compares the responses of the die with those of the netlist.
Most chips are tested twice. The wafer test contacts the pads of each die with the needles of a probe card before the wafer is sawn, and the failing dies are recorded in a wafer map and never packaged. The final test repeats the test after packaging, because sawing, bonding, and molding add defects of their own. Parts for cars or medical devices often also run a burn-in at raised temperature and supply voltage, which makes weak parts fail before they are shipped. The tester, called automatic test equipment (ATE), applies the test: in every clock cycle, it drives a vector onto the inputs and compares the outputs with the expected values. Tester time is expensive, so the test of a die takes seconds at most, and every vector counts.
A defect that escapes the test costs more the later it is found. A rule of thumb says that the cost grows by about a factor of ten from step to step: on the wafer, in the package, on the board, and in the system of the customer, where a defective part in a car can mean a recall. The fault coverage \(T\) of a test is the share of the modeled faults that it detects (Section 9.3). With less than 100 %, some defective dies pass. The defect level \(DL\), the share of defective dies among those that pass the test, follows from the yield and the coverage in the model of Williams and Brown (Williams and Brown 1981):
\[
DL = 1 - Y^{1-T}
\]
With 80 % yield and 99 % coverage, 0.22 % of the shipped dies are defective, 2229 parts per million (ppm), or one in 449 (Figure 35). Customers in the automotive industry ask for defect levels of a few ppm. Even for 100 ppm at 80 % yield, the coverage must reach \(T = 1 - \ln(1 - DL)/\ln Y\) = 99.955 %, and at a lower yield, more still.








Figure 35: Defect level \(DL = 1 - Y^{1-T}\), the fraction of shipped dies that are defective, over the fault coverage \(T\) of the test from 95 to 100 %, for four values of the yield \(Y\). At 80 % yield and 99 % coverage, 0.22 % of the shipped dies are defective (dot), one in 449.

title: VLSI Design
text:
9.3 Fault Models
A test cannot target physical defects directly: their number is endless, and their effect depends on the layout. Instead, it targets faults, models of defects on the netlist that a tool can list and simulate (Bushnell and Agrawal 2000).
The stuck-at fault model assumes that a net or a pin of a cell is fixed at 0 (stuck-at-0, s-a-0) or at 1 (stuck-at-1, s-a-1), while all cells keep their functions. The single stuck-at model assumes one fault at a time, so \(n\) fault sites give \(2n\) faults, whereas multiple faults would give \(3^n - 1\) combinations. The model is simple, yet a test that detects all single stuck-at faults also detects many other defects, because a short or an open usually forces some net to a wrong value for some input. The tool Fault of Section 9.4 counts every pin of every cell and every port bit, except the clock and the reset input, as a fault site.
Many faults are equivalent, i.e., exactly the same tests detect them. A stuck-at-1 at an input of an OR gate forces its output to 1, just like a stuck-at-1 at the output. Tools merge equivalent faults, which shortens the list (fault collapsing). Some faults cannot be detected at all, because no input makes the faulty circuit behave differently from the good one, e.g., in redundant logic. Such a fault is untestable, like an equivalent mutant in Section 4.9. The fault coverage counts all faults, the test coverage leaves out the untestable ones, so it reaches 100 % when every detectable fault is detected.
Other fault models and test methods capture defects that the stuck-at model misses:

Transition faults model a gate that is too slow: its output rises (slow-to-rise) or falls (slow-to-fall) too late. Their test needs two vectors: the first sets the old value, the second launches the transition, and the response is captured one clock period later, at the speed of the chip (Section 9.7). Path delay faults model the delay of a whole path.
Bridging faults short two nets. The result depends on the drivers: the stronger one wins, or the bridge acts like an AND or an OR of both nets. A test drives the two nets to opposite values.
Stuck-open faults model a transistor that never conducts. For some inputs, the output of the CMOS gate then floats and keeps its last value, so the gate turns into a memory, and the test needs two vectors.
IDDQ testing measures the quiescent supply current. A CMOS circuit at rest draws only its leakage current. A defect that connects the supply to ground in some states only, e.g., a bridge between two nets driven to opposite values, raises the current far above that in these states, which a current measurement after a few vectors finds, even when no output shows a wrong value. In large chips of modern processes, the leakage itself is high and varies from die to die, which hides the extra current.

title: VLSI Design
text:
9.4 Test Generation
A test vector for a fault, or simply a test, is an input vector for which the faulty circuit gives a different output from the good one. Finding one takes three steps. Excite the fault, i.e., drive the fault site to the value opposite to the stuck value. Propagate the difference along a path to an output, by setting every other input of each gate on the path to its non-controlling value, 1 for AND and NAND gates, 0 for OR and NOR gates. Justify all these internal values from the inputs. Figure 36 shows a test found this way. A value such as 1/0 stands for 1 in the good and 0 in the faulty circuit.








Figure 36: A test for the stuck-at-0 fault at the output of the inverter. c = 0 excites the fault: the net is 1 in the good circuit and 0 in the faulty one (1/0). d = 1 lets the NAND gate pass the difference, and a = b = 0 let the NOR gate pass it. The test vector (a, b, c, d) = (0, 0, 0, 1) gives y = 1 in the good and y = 0 in the faulty circuit.





Exciting and propagating need controllability and observability: how easily a net can be set to a value from the inputs, and how easily its value can be seen at an output. Nets behind many levels of logic are hard to control and hard to observe. Justification fails when two required values conflict. The classic algorithms of automatic test pattern generation (ATPG), the D-algorithm and PODEM, then go back and try other assignments, and when every alternative fails, the fault is untestable.
Modern tools often hand this search to a SAT solver, the same kind of solver as in the equivalence check of Section 5.8. A miter joins the good and the faulty netlist: both get the same inputs, an XOR compares each pair of outputs, and the solver searches for an input that sets one of the XORs to 1. Every solution is a test, and if there is none, the fault is proven untestable. The script sat_test.tcl does this with Yosys for one fault: it ties the listed cell pins to the stuck value in a copy of the netlist, builds the miter, and lets the command sat search:


atpg/sat_test.tcl

# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Simon Dorrer
# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
# Description: Test generation for one stuck-at fault with a SAT
# solver. Builds a copy of the netlist with the fault, joins both in a
# miter, and searches an input for which the outputs differ. Usage:
#   TOP=cons PINS=u_or/C SA=0 yosys -c sat_test.tcl
# TOP is the module, read from $TOP.v unless NETLIST names the file.
# PINS lists the cell inputs that the fault forces to SA: one pin for
# a net with one load, all its loads for a net with several. (This
# misses a net that also drives an output port.)

yosys -import
set top $::env(TOP)
set netlist $top.v
if {[info exists ::env(NETLIST)]} { set netlist $::env(NETLIST) }
set lib $::env(PDK_ROOT)/ihp-sg13cmos5l/libs.ref/sg13cmos5l_stdcell
set lib $lib/lib/sg13cmos5l_stdcell_typ_1p20V_25C.lib

# The cell functions from the Liberty file, then the netlist
read_liberty -ignore_miss_func $lib
read_verilog $netlist
hierarchy -check -top $top

# The faulty copy: each listed pin is tied to the stuck-at value
copy $top faulty
yosys cd faulty
foreach p $::env(PINS) {
  lassign [split $p /] cell pin
  connect -port $cell $pin 1'b$::env(SA)
}
yosys cd ..

# The miter compares both copies, the solver searches a difference
miter -equiv -flatten -make_outputs $top faulty miter
hierarchy -top miter
tee -q -o sat.log sat -prove trigger 0 -show-inputs miter
set f [open sat.log]
set log [read $f]
close $f
if {[string match "*model found: FAIL*" $log]} {
  puts "TEST FOUND, the inputs (decimal):"
  set rows {^\s+\\in_(\S+)\s+(\d+)}
  foreach {- name value} [regexp -all -inline -line $rows $log] {
    puts "  $name = $value"
  }
} else {
  puts "NO TEST EXISTS: the fault is untestable"
}


Applying all input vectors would detect every detectable fault, but as in Section 4.6.2, their number explodes. The combinational 32-bit barrel shifter of Section 4 has 39 input bits, i.e., \(2^{39} \approx 5.5 \cdot 10^{11}\) vectors, which take 1.5 hours per die at 100 MHz. Fortunately, most faults are easy to detect, and a few random vectors find them. Fault simulation determines which faults a vector detects: it simulates the netlist with each fault injected and compares the outputs with those of the good netlist. ATPG tools therefore start with random vectors, drop the faults these detect, and search deterministically only for the rest. Some faults resist random vectors. The output of a 16-bit comparator with a constant is 1 for one of \(2^{16}\) input values, so 1000 random vectors detect its stuck-at-0 with a probability of only 1.5 %, and a probability of 99 % would take \(3.0 \cdot 10^5\) vectors. The deterministic search finds the single test at once. Finally, compaction removes vectors whose faults other vectors detect as well.
The IIC-OSIC-TOOLS image contains Fault (AUCOHL 2026) 0.9.4, an open-source DFT tool chain. fault atpg generates random vectors in batches, -v vectors at first and -r more in each further batch, simulates all faults with Icarus Verilog, and continues until it reaches the coverage that -m demands or the number of vectors that --ceiling allows. Then it compacts the vectors. It injects each fault with a force on a cell pin. Fault can also call deterministic ATPG programs, but none of them is available in the image, so here it relies on random vectors, and sat_test.tcl handles single faults.






TipExercise: Find the Test



All commands start in the folder content/dft/code/atpg, which holds the gate-level netlist cons.v of SG13CMOS5L cells.

Draw the circuit of cons.v with its cell instances and net names, and write down its function \(y = f(a, b, c)\) as a sum of products. Which product could you remove without changing the function?
Find by hand a test for each of these faults: ab stuck-at-0, a_n stuck-at-1, bc stuck-at-1, and bc stuck-at-0. Which values does each one need to be excited and propagated? If you find no test, explain why none exists.
Check your answers with the SAT solver. A fault on a net with one load needs only that load pin, e.g., for ab stuck-at-0:
TOP=cons PINS=u_or/A SA=0 yosys -q -c sat_test.tcl
Which pins does a stuck-at fault on the input b_i need? Is a stuck-at-0 at the pin A of u_bc alone testable?
Let Fault generate a test set:
fault atpg cons.v -c $CELLS/sg13cmos5l_stdcell.v \
  -I $CELLS/sg13cmos5l_udp.v --clock clk_i --reset rst_ni \
  --activeLow -v 8 -m 100 --ceiling 32 -o cons.tv.json \
  --output-coverage-metadata cons.cov.yml
How many fault sites and faults does Fault find, and which coverage does it reach? Which faults stay undetected (the list sa0Uncovered in cons.cov.yml, the list sa1Uncovered of Fault 0.9.4 repeats it by mistake)? How many vectors remain after the compaction, which ones are they (cons.tv.json), and could fewer vectors detect the same faults? Does Fault agree with step 3 on the pin A of u_bc?



Before continuing, please finish the previous exercise. Once you are done, compare with the solution below.






TipSolution: Find the Test






The circuit (Figure 37) computes \(y = ab + \bar{a}c + bc\). The product \(bc\) is the consensus of the other two and can be removed: for \(b = c = 1\), either \(a = 1\) and \(ab = 1\), or \(a = 0\) and \(\bar{a}c = 1\). So \(y = ab + \bar{a}c\).









Figure 37: The netlist cons.v: \(y = ab + \bar{a}c + bc\). The term \(bc\) is the consensus of the other two: whenever \(b = c = 1\), either \(ab\) or \(\bar{a}c\) is 1 as well, so the gate u_bc never changes the output.






With the inputs written as \((a, b, c)\):

ab stuck-at-0: excite with \(a = b = 1\). To pass the OR gate, anc and bc must be 0: anc is 0 because a_n is 0, and bc = 0 needs \(c = 0\). The test is (1, 1, 0), with \(y\) = 1 in the good and 0 in the faulty circuit.
a_n stuck-at-1: excite with a_n = 0, i.e., \(a = 1\). Propagate through u_anc with \(c = 1\) and through u_or with ab = 0, i.e., \(b = 0\), which also keeps bc at 0. The test is (1, 0, 1).
bc stuck-at-1: excite with bc = 0 and propagate with ab = anc = 0, i.e., any input with \(y\) = 0 in the good circuit: (0, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0), (1, 0, 0), or (1, 0, 1).
bc stuck-at-0: excite with \(b = c = 1\). To propagate, ab = 0 needs \(a = 0\), and anc = 0 needs a_n = 0, i.e., \(a = 1\). The two requirements conflict, so no test exists: the fault is untestable, because bc is redundant.

The solver confirms all four: it prints (1, 1, 0) for PINS=u_or/A SA=0, (1, 0, 1) for PINS=u_anc/A SA=1, (0, 0, 0) for PINS=u_or/C SA=1, and “NO TEST EXISTS” for PINS=u_or/C SA=0. A fault on b_i acts on both cells it drives, so it needs PINS="u_ab/B u_bc/A". The solver finds (1, 1, 1) for stuck-at-0 and (1, 0, 0) for stuck-at-1. A stuck-at-0 at the pin A of u_bc alone forces bc to 0, like bc stuck-at-0, and is untestable as well.
Fault finds 19 fault sites, the 15 cell pins and the 4 ports a_i, b_i, c_i, and y_o (it leaves out clk_i and rst_ni), i.e., 38 faults, and reaches 94.74 %, 36 of 38. The two undetected faults, the stuck-at-0 at u_bc.X and at u_or.C, are both the untestable stuck-at-0 on the net bc. The compaction keeps 4 vectors: (0, 0, 1), (1, 0, 1), (0, 1, 0), and (1, 1, 0). Fewer cannot detect the same faults: ab stuck-at-0 has the single test (1, 1, 0), because in (1, 1, 1) bc = 1 hides the fault. anc stuck-at-0 has the single test (0, 0, 1), and a_n stuck-at-1 the single test (1, 0, 1). The input c_i stuck-at-1 needs \(a = c = 0\), which none of these three vectors has. Fault reports the stuck-at-0 at the pin A of u_bc as detected, which step 3 proved untestable. Fault forces the pin, and Icarus merges the input pin of a cell with the net it connects to when the net has one bit. The force thus acts on the whole net b_i, its stem, instead of its branch to u_bc alone, so the fault that Fault simulates is b_i stuck-at-0, which (1, 1, 0) detects. Commercial ATPG tools list the stem and every branch of a net as separate faults.

title: VLSI Design
text:
9.5 Scan Design
In a sequential circuit, the logic between the registers is reachable only through the registers. To test a gate inside a state machine, a test must first steer the machine into a state that excites the fault, and then wait until the difference reaches an output, over many clock cycles. Sequential ATPG exists, but it is slow, and in large designs, its coverage stays low.
Scan design makes every flip-flop controllable and observable. Each flip-flop becomes a scan flip-flop, with a multiplexer in front of its input (Figure 38). With the scan enable low, it loads its functional input. With the scan enable high, it loads the output of the previous flip-flop in the chain, and all scan flip-flops together form a shift register, the scan chain, from an input pin scan_in to an output pin scan_out. The tester can now shift any state into the flip-flops, and shift out any state they captured. For the test generation, the output Q of each flip-flop becomes an input of the logic, and its input D an output, so the sequential problem turns into the combinational one of Section 9.4.








Figure 38: Scan design. (a) A scan flip-flop such as sdfrbpq_1 is a flip-flop with a multiplexer in front: with SCE = 0, it loads the functional input D, with SCE = 1 the scan input SCD. (b) The scan flip-flops of a design form a shift register, the scan chain (orange), from scan_in through every flip-flop to scan_out. One scan_enable switches all of them between shifting and normal operation.





SG13CMOS5L has five scan flip-flops (Section 5.3): sdfrbpq_1 and sdfrbpq_2 with the output Q, sdfrbp_1 and sdfrbp_2 with Q and Q_N, and sdfbbp_1 with set and reset. Their scan input is SCD, their scan enable SCE. sdfrbpq_1 takes 63.5 µm², 30 % more than dfrbpq_1 with 49.0 µm², but less than dfrbpq_1 and mux2_1 together (67.1 µm²). The Liberty file describes the scan function of each cell in a test_cell group, from which tools learn which pin is the scan input and which flip-flop it can replace.
Figure 39 shows how the tester applies the patterns one after the other. A scan pattern is a test vector arranged for the scan test: the values of the flip-flops in the order in which they are shifted in, and the values of the primary inputs, the inputs of the design itself. While scan_enable is high, every clock edge shifts the chain by one bit, so after \(L\) edges, a chain of \(L\) flip-flops holds the pattern. The tester applies the primary inputs, compares the primary outputs, sets scan_enable low, and gives one clock edge, the capture, at which every flip-flop loads the response of the logic. The next \(L\) shift edges unload this response at scan_out while they load the next pattern, and the tester compares each bit with its expected value. Before the first pattern, a test program runs a chain test: it shifts a known sequence such as 0011… through the chain without a capture and checks that it arrives unchanged at scan_out.








Figure 39: A scan test with a chain of four flip-flops. While scan_enable is high, every rising clock edge shifts the chain by one position, so four edges load pattern 1 from scan_in. In the capture cycle, scan_enable is low, and the edge at its end (dashed) captures the response of the logic to the pattern and to the primary inputs. The next four shift edges unload the response at scan_out and load pattern 2 at the same time.





For \(N\) patterns and a chain of \(L\) flip-flops, the test takes \((N + 1) L + N\) clock cycles: \(N + 1\) shift phases of \(L\) cycles, because the last response must come out as well, and \(N\) captures. The shifts dominate, so designs split their flip-flops into several chains that shift in parallel, each with its own pins. When the pins run out, on-chip test compression feeds hundreds of short chains from a few pins through a decompressor and compacts their outputs. The shift clock is often slower than the functional clock, because shifting random patterns toggles many more flip-flops at once than normal operation, which draws a high current.
In the open-source flow, OpenROAD (The OpenROAD Project 2026) inserts the chains. scan_replace replaces every flip-flop by a scan flip-flop with the same function, and execute_dft_plan stitches the chains and adds the ports scan_enable_0, scan_in_0, scan_out_0, and so on. In a complete flow, scan_replace runs before the placement, because it changes the cell areas, and execute_dft_plan after it, so that each chain connects neighbors on the die. The script dft.tcl runs both on a netlist without placement:


scan/dft.tcl

# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Simon Dorrer
# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
# Description: Scan insertion with OpenROAD. Replaces every flip-flop
# by its scan version and stitches the scan chains. Usage, in the
# folder of the netlist: TOP=bs_reg openroad -no_init -exit dft.tcl
# (reads $TOP.nl.v, writes ${TOP}_scan.nl.v). CLOCKS lists the clock
# inputs (default clk_i), MAX_LENGTH limits the length of a chain
# (default 100).

set top $::env(TOP)
set clocks clk_i
if {[info exists ::env(CLOCKS)]} { set clocks $::env(CLOCKS) }
set max_length 100
if {[info exists ::env(MAX_LENGTH)]} {
  set max_length $::env(MAX_LENGTH)
}

set lib $::env(PDK_ROOT)/ihp-sg13cmos5l/libs.ref/sg13cmos5l_stdcell
read_lef $lib/lef/sg13cmos5l_tech.lef
read_lef $lib/lef/sg13cmos5l_stdcell.lef
read_liberty $lib/lib/sg13cmos5l_stdcell_typ_1p20V_25C.lib
read_verilog $top.nl.v
link_design $top

# The chains are built per clock, so the clocks must be known
foreach clk $clocks {
  create_clock -name $clk -period 100 [get_ports $clk]
}
set_dft_config -max_length $max_length -clock_mixing no_mix

# Replace the flip-flops, plan the chains, and stitch them
scan_replace
report_dft_plan -verbose
execute_dft_plan
write_verilog ${top}_scan.nl.v


LibreLane, the flow of Section 10, has no step for scan insertion. For the test generation, fault cut turns each flip-flop into an input and an output, and fault atpg generates vectors for the result. The file scl.yml tells Fault which cells are flip-flops. The following commands synthesize the barrel shifter between two registers of Section 6.7 with 8 bits instead of 32, cut its flip-flops open, and generate vectors:
cd /foss/designs/vlsi-design/content/dft/code/scan
yosys -p "read_verilog -sv \
  ../../../verification/code/barrel_shift/rtl/barrel_shift.sv \
  ../../../sequential/code/bs_reg/rtl/bs_reg.sv; \
  chparam -set WIDTH 8 bs_reg; synth -top bs_reg; flatten; \
  dfflibmap -liberty $LIB; abc -constr $CONSTR -liberty $LIB; \
  opt_clean; stat -liberty $LIB; write_verilog -noattr bs_reg.nl.v"
fault cut bs_reg.nl.v --sclConfig scl.yml --clock clk_i \
  --reset rst_ni --activeLow -o bs_reg.cut.v
fault atpg bs_reg.cut.v -c $CELLS/sg13cmos5l_stdcell.v \
  -I $CELLS/sg13cmos5l_udp.v --clock clk_i --reset rst_ni \
  --activeLow -v 100 -r 100 -m 100 --ceiling 1000 \
  -o bs_reg.tv.json
Fault holds the reset inactive and finds 580 fault sites, i.e., 1160 faults. Figure 40 shows how the coverage grows with the number of random vectors: 97.84 % after 100 vectors and 99.66 % from 350 on. The four faults that remain are not missed by chance: sat_test.tcl proves each of them untestable, because ABC left redundant logic in the netlist. In the fault model of Fault, the test coverage is therefore 100 %. After 1000 vectors, Fault stops at its ceiling and compacts the set to 32 vectors that detect the same 1156 faults.








Figure 40: Stuck-at fault coverage of random test vectors for the 8-bit bs_reg, with its flip-flops cut into inputs and outputs, simulated by Fault with -v 10 -r 10, i.e., in batches of 10 vectors. Most faults are detected within the first 50 vectors. From 350 vectors on, all 1156 faults that the fault model of Fault can detect are found. The other 4 of the 1160 faults are untestable, so the coverage stays at 99.66 %.





Coverage numbers depend on the fault model. Fault injects a fault with a force on a cell pin. Icarus merges the input pin of a cell with the net it connects to when the net has one bit, so the force acts on the whole net, the stem. A force on a pin at one bit of a vector acts on that pin alone, the branch of the net to this cell. In this netlist, 300 of the 379 inputs of the logic cells sit on nets of one bit, so Fault mostly simulates faults on whole nets, where commercial ATPG tools list the stem and every branch as separate faults. In a fault simulation with a wire of its own for every cell input, the 32 vectors miss 59 of the 1034 faults at the pins of the 138 logic cells. The SAT solver proves 12 of them untestable, and the other 47 would need more vectors, so the test coverage at the cell pins is 95.4 %.
The scan flip-flop also costs speed. On the worst path of the 8-bit bs_reg between two registers, its setup time is 0.204 ns instead of 0.125 ns for dfrbpq_1, and its clock-to-output delay 0.344 ns instead of 0.309 ns. The gates on the path take 0.019 ns longer, mainly because the last of them drives the larger input D of the scan flip-flop. The minimum period rises from 1.30 to 1.43 ns.






TipExercise: Insert a Scan Chain



All commands start in the folder content/dft/code/scan and use bs_reg.nl.v and bs_reg.tv.json from the commands above.

Sketch the registers of the 8-bit bs_reg with their widths and draw a scan chain through all of their flip-flops. How long is the chain?
Insert the chain with TOP=bs_reg openroad -no_init -exit dft.tcl. In which order does OpenROAD chain the registers, and which flip-flop drives scan_out_0? Compare the area of bs_reg.nl.v and bs_reg_scan.nl.v:
yosys -p "read_liberty -lib $LIB; read_verilog bs_reg_scan.nl.v; \
  stat -liberty $LIB"
How much area does the scan insertion add in total and in percent, and which cells changed?
Convert the vectors of Fault into scan patterns and run the scan test of tb/tb_scan.sv:
python3 scan_patterns.py bs_reg_scan.nl.v bs_reg.tv.json > bs_reg.pat
iverilog -g2012 -gno-specify -DPATTERNS=\"bs_reg.pat\" -o scan.vvp \
  $CELLS/sg13cmos5l_udp.v $CELLS/sg13cmos5l_stdcell.v \
  bs_reg_scan.nl.v tb/tb_scan.sv
vvp -n scan.vvp
What do the chain test and the scan test report? Where do the expected responses come from?
Inject a defect: compile again with -DFAULT=_007_ -DSA=0 added, then with -DFAULT=_008_ -DSA=1. Which defect does the scan test detect, and why not the other one? Repeat both with random patterns, i.e., without -DPATTERNS=.... What changes, and why?
The tester shifts at 10 MHz. How long does the scan test of the 32 patterns take with one chain? Build three chains of at most 7 flip-flops instead with MAX_LENGTH=7 TOP=bs_reg openroad -no_init -exit dft.tcl (it overwrites bs_reg_scan.nl.v). How long does the test take then?



Before continuing, please finish the previous exercise. Once you are done, compare with the solution below.






TipSolution: Insert a Scan Chain






bs_reg has the registers data_q (8 bits), shamt_q (3 bits), mode_q (2 bits), and out_q (8 bits), so the chain has 21 flip-flops (Figure 41).









Figure 41: The 8-bit bs_reg after scan insertion. Top: its registers in normal operation. Bottom: the same 21 flip-flops as one scan chain (orange), from scan_in_0 through mode_q, shamt_q, out_q, and data_q, each from its highest bit to its lowest, to scan_out_0, the output of data_q[0]. scan_enable_0 drives all 21 SCE pins (not drawn).






Without a placement, OpenROAD has no wire lengths to minimize, and here it chains the flip-flops in descending order of their instance names, from _288_ at scan_in_0 to _268_ at scan_out_0: mode_q, shamt_q, out_q, and data_q, each from its highest bit to its lowest. scan_out_0 is connected directly to data_q[0], the output of _268_, and each SCD to the output of the previous flip-flop, without any additional cell. The area grows from 2543.45 to 2848.27 µm², by 304.82 µm² or 12.0 %, and only the flip-flops changed: each of the 21 became an sdfrbpq_1, 14.52 µm² larger than dfrbpq_1.
scan_patterns.py follows the chain from scan_in_0 and reports its 21 flip-flops. The chain test reports 0 of 21 bits wrong, and the scan test 32 patterns with 0 bits that differ. The expected responses come from the second instance gold of the same netlist, which is fault-free and receives the same patterns, just as a test program takes its expected values from a simulation of the fault-free netlist. The file of Fault also holds the fault-free response of each vector (goldenOutput), but the testbench does not use it.
With _007_ stuck-at-0, one bit differs, so the scan test detects it. _008_ stuck-at-1 stays undetected: _008_ is the output of _253_ and drives only the input A2 of _254_, and its stuck-at-1 is one of the four untestable faults, together with both faults at the input B of _253_ and the stuck-at-1 at A2 of _254_. With 32 random patterns, _007_ stuck-at-0 stays undetected too, and no bit differs: none of the random patterns excites the fault and propagates it to a flip-flop. Fault selected its 32 vectors from 1000 random ones, so that together they detect every fault that it could detect.
One chain: \((32 + 1) \cdot 21 + 32 = 725\) cycles, i.e., 72.5 µs at 10 MHz. Three chains of 7 flip-flops: \((32 + 1) \cdot 7 + 32 = 263\) cycles, i.e., 26.3 µs.




Scan insertion changes the netlist, so the equivalence check of Section 5.8 runs after it. With the scan inputs tied to 0, the scanned netlist must compute exactly what the netlist before scan insertion computed. The script scan_eq.tcl checks this with the Yosys commands equiv_make, equiv_simple, and equiv_induct. They match the nets of both netlists by name, among them the outputs of all flip-flops, and prove each matched pair, a point of the check, equal. After the exercise, bs_reg_scan.nl.v holds the netlist with three chains, and TOP=bs_reg yosys -q -c scan_eq.tcl in the folder scan proves all 163 points of bs_reg equal, as it does for the netlist with one chain. With the scan inputs tied to 1 (TIE=1), the check fails: 32 points of the netlist with three chains and 38 of the one with one chain cannot be proven equal.

title: VLSI Design
text:
9.6 Design Rules for Testability
Scan works only if the tester controls the design in test mode. Every flip-flop must shift and capture at the clock of the tester, nothing may disturb the chain while it shifts, and the logic must give values that the ATPG can predict. ATPG tools check rules for this before they generate any pattern. The most important rules:

Every clock comes from a pin. In test mode, the tester drives all clocks. A clock from a divider (Section 3.4.2), from a phase-locked loop (PLL), or from another flip-flop (Section 6.8) needs a multiplexer that selects a clock pin in test mode. A clock enable, which replaces the divider in Section 3.4.2, needs nothing. At-speed tests take faster pulses from an on-chip PLL, through a clock controller that the tester controls (Section 9.7).
Every clock gate has a test enable. An integrated clock gate (Section 7.7) switches off the clock while its enable is low, and the enable comes from logic whose flip-flops are shifting, so the gated flip-flops would miss shift edges. The clock gate slgcp_1 (30.8 µm², against 27.2 µm² for lgcp_1) therefore has the input SCE. The cell ORs SCE with GATE in front of the latch (latch_posedge_precontrol), and the Liberty file marks SCE as clock_gate_test_pin. Connected to the scan enable, it turns on every gated clock while the chain shifts. Clock gating is thus fine for scan, as long as the test enable is connected. Neither Yosys nor OpenROAD connects it to the scan enable. For cg_reg of Section 7.7 with WIDTH = 8, clockgate connects only GATE, CLK, and GCLK of slgcp_1, or ties SCE to 0 with -tie_lo SCE. OpenROAD puts the 8 gated flip-flops into a chain, warns that the clock gate is not a scan cell, and leaves SCE unconnected.
Asynchronous resets are controlled from a pin. The tester holds a reset from a pin inactive during the whole test. A reset that the design generates itself, e.g., in a power-on-reset circuit, in the reset synchronizer of Section 8.8, or from another flip-flop, needs special care in test mode. The following exercise shows why.
No latches, no combinational loops, no pulse generators. A latch passes or holds depending on its gate, so it is neither a clean input nor a clean output for the ATPG. Latches are made transparent in test mode, or the design uses flip-flops only (Section 6.11). The latch inside a clock gate is the exception, because its test enable controls it. A combinational loop has no defined value and is broken in test mode. A pulse generator built from a delay chain, e.g., an XOR of a signal and its delayed copy, gives pulses whose width depends on the process, which scan cannot test.
No unknown values reach a flip-flop. Memories (Section 3.4.3), analog blocks, and black boxes give values that the ATPG cannot predict (x), and an x captured in a flip-flop makes its bit of the response useless. A tri-state bus (Section 3.4.4) floats or has two active drivers when a shifted state enables none or two of them. Such blocks get a bypass or a wrapper of scan flip-flops in test mode, and memories a test of their own (Section 9.7).
One chain per clock domain. Flip-flops of different clocks see their edges at different moments, so a chain should not mix them. With -clock_mixing no_mix, OpenROAD builds one chain per clock. For the asynchronous FIFO of Section 8.6, it builds a chain of 43 flip-flops at wclk_i and one of 11 at rclk_i, which share scan_enable_0. A chain that crosses from one clock to another needs a lockup latch at the crossing, a latch on the launching clock that is transparent while this clock is low. It delays the data by half a period, so that a skew of up to about half a period between the clocks cannot cause a hold violation. During the capture, the paths between asynchronous clocks are not timed (Section 8.7), so their results are unknown when both clocks pulse. The ATPG then captures one clock domain at a time, or ignores the flip-flops behind such paths, e.g., the first stage of each synchronizer.
The chain is a timing path, too. The connection from Q to the SCD of the next flip-flop has no logic, so it is among the shortest paths of a design and the first to fail the hold check when the clock reaches the next flip-flop late (Section 6.10). In the scanned 8-bit bs_reg, the 20 paths with the smallest hold slack all end at an SCD pin, from 0.292 ns with an ideal clock, which already includes the clock uncertainty of 0.1 ns, while the functional paths start at 0.383 ns. A clock skew of 0.3 ns between two neighbors in the chain would violate the hold check, and from about 0.39 ns, the chain itself would fail. After the clock tree synthesis, the layout flow fixes hold violations on the scan paths like on any other path, with delay cells. scan_enable_0 drives all 21 SCE pins, a net with a high fanout like a reset, which must settle within one shift cycle.







TipExercise: Make It Testable



All commands start in the folder content/dft/code/reset. It holds the reference solution rtl/bs_reg_rs_tm.sv, so move it out of the way first: cd /foss/designs/vlsi-design/content/dft/code/reset, then mv rtl/bs_reg_rs_tm.sv bs_reg_rs_tm_solution.sv.

Synthesize bs_reg_rs with 8 bits, insert a scan chain, and run the scan test:
